item.title: Provo food bank closure leaves gaps as community steps up to help
item.description:
The closure of Provo's Community Action Services and Food Bank has cut off regular deliveries to many of Alpine School District's 15 school food pantries heading into Thanksgiving. Tabitha's Way, which previously didn't serve Orem, will now open to Orem families and helped district staff assemble 1,167 holiday meals, 500 of them for district families.

Orem Junior High pantry coordinator Sandi Nelson said "families don't know where they can go and get food," and that the pantry lacks fresh produce, milk and eggs. District leaders said the school pantries still need donations to stay stocked in the coming weeks.

item.title: Immigrant detained in Provo for allegedly distributing stickers with messages targeting Trump
item.description:
Federal agents arrested Venezuelan immigrant Hector Alejandro Mujica-Hernandez in Provo in October over stickers he allegedly handed out urging people to shoot President Donald Trump, the Department of Homeland Security said Monday. He was being held at an ICE detention center in Louisiana as of Monday, and online federal court records showed no criminal charges against him.

DHS says he entered the country legally in 2016 and overstayed his visa, and Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the department "will not tolerate death threats of any kind." A GoFundMe linked from the Instagram page of People of Provo Against ICE, the group at whose meeting DHS says the stickers were distributed, calls him "a pillar to our community" and seeks help with his legal costs.

  • Immigrant detained in Provo for allegedly distributing stickers with messages targeting Trump - ksl.com

item.title: Rivals unite to support Mountain Ridge basketball star battling cancer
item.description:
Varsity players from six rival high schools gathered at Mountain Ridge High in Herriman on Monday for a three-point shooting contest to raise money for Sentinels guard Spencer Perry, 18, who has Hodgkin lymphoma. Perry plans to keep playing as much as he can, starting with Tuesday night's game, before chemotherapy begins Dec. 7.

Teams sank 200 shots, each one adding to the fund for Perry's family. Doctors have offered encouraging news, and Perry said, "It's not super scary because it's a really well-treated cancer."

item.title: Batmobile stalls at auction by failing to meet the seller's minimum price
item.description:
A Batmobile built for Tim Burton's 1992 film Batman Returns went unsold at a Julien's auction Monday after bidding stalled at $3.25 million, below the seller's reserve. Julien's had estimated the car at $5 million to $7 million and hoped it would top the $4.6 million Batmobile record set in 2013.

A buyer would also have faced limits under an agreement with Warner Bros., such as keeping it "stationary when exhibited to the public" and getting approval for special events. Julien's called the car, one of three built for the film, "one of the most recognized and important cinematic vehicles in Hollywood history."

  • Batmobile stalls at auction by failing to meet the seller's minimum price - ksl.com

item.title: Your flight was canceled. Who pays for dinner or the hotel?
item.description:
Under a federal Transportation Department rule, travelers whose flight is canceled, or whose domestic flight is expected to land three or more hours late, are owed an automatic refund if they decide not to fly. Help with meals and hotels is less certain and depends on each airline's own policies, and sometimes on the credit card used to buy the ticket.

Delta, which has a Salt Lake City hub, promises meals after three-hour delays within its control and hotel rooms for passengers stranded overnight. Katy Nastro of the Flighty app said the refund rule applies whether the cause is weather, an FAA ground stop or an airline's own decision.

  • Your flight was canceled. Who pays for dinner or the hotel? - ksl.com

item.title: Utah lawmakers eye another attempt to repeal law allowing developers to form cities
item.description:
A Utah legislative interim committee on Wednesday endorsed outgoing lawmaker Tiara Auxier's draft bill to fully repeal SB258, the 2024 pilot program letting private landowners in largely undeveloped areas petition to start new municipalities. Because Auxier lost her reelection bid, another legislator is likely to carry the bill when the general session opens in January.

As drafted, the repeal would also dissolve preliminary municipalities already approved, such as Echo Canyon in Grand County. Ivory Development president Chris Gamvroulas defended the law as an escape from "weaponized county government," while Sen. Calvin Musselman, who voted no, predicted, "A repeal is going to happen."


Sources:

  • Utah lawmakers eye another attempt to repeal law allowing developers to form cities - ksl.com

item.title: Utah man convicted of murder now accused of attacking officer at state prison
item.description:
Erik Orozco, 23, who pleaded guilty in 2022 to an Ogden murder and is already in prison, was charged Monday with aggravated assault targeting law enforcement and possessing a weapon as an inmate. Charging documents allege he came at a corrections officer from behind with a makeshift cutting weapon on July 26, leaving the officer with head lacerations; the officer was treated at a hospital.

The case is separate from a September attack on an officer at the Gunnison prison that led to a monthlong lockdown at two state facilities. According to the charges, Orozco told investigators he was "sick of how they were treating them and of the disrespect".

item.title: New federal rule ends housing aid for some families
item.description:
A U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule finalized Nov. 10 will require every member of a household receiving federal housing aid to be verified as a citizen or eligible noncitizen starting Dec. 14. Mixed-status families that now pay higher rent to cover ineligible relatives will lose that option, and opponents estimate about 80,000 people could be displaced.

HUD Secretary Scott Turner said American taxpayers "will no longer foot the bill," but the department's own regulatory analysis projects no savings and up to $251 million in costs. Landlords get 90 days after the rule takes effect to comply.

item.title: Cache County School District receives $990K grant to improve student literacy
item.description:
Intermountain Health has given the Cache County School District a three-year, $990,000 grant to strengthen reading and literacy programs across its schools. The district aims to have every third grader reading at benchmark by 2030, up from about 80% today.

Tabitha Bishop of Intermountain's Community Care Foundation said the plan stood out because it reached beyond students and educators to families and the wider community, calling it "really innovative and well thought out". District communications director Sheri Anderson said students who struggle to read find learning in subjects like health and science harder.

  • Cache County School District receives $990K grant to improve student literacy - ksl.com

item.title: Woman threatens to blow up trailer during standoff with police
item.description:
Beryl resident Brenda Tallerico, 58, was charged Monday with assaulting officers and other counts after allegedly threatening to blow up her trailer during a Sunday standoff with Iron County deputies. Deputies cut power and gas to the trailer, used chemical agents and finally breached the door to arrest her.

According to the affidavit, a relative told police she claimed to be filling the trailer with gas while waiting at the door with a torch. Her blood-alcohol level measured 0.34% at a hospital, and deputies reported finding "a large bundle of burnt matches" inside.

  • Woman threatens to blow up trailer during standoff with police - ksl.com

item.title: Utah board votes unanimously to certify the midterm election results
item.description:
Utah's State Board of Canvassers unanimously certified the general election results Monday, making official a vote that cost Republicans their supermajority in the Utah House. The GOP keeps control of both chambers, but after losing 16 House seats it will be without a veto-proof majority for the first time in close to three decades.

Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, whom several Republicans including Phil Lyman had asked to postpone certification, said the concerns they raised had "no merit". She said more than 90% of voters returned ballots by mail or drop box, adding that Utahns "prefer vote-by-mail".

  • Utah board votes unanimously to certify the midterm election results - ksl.com

item.title: A stunning supermoon peaks this week. Here's what to know
item.description:
November's beaver moon, the first of three supermoons in a row, reaches peak fullness Tuesday morning, though NASA's Noah Petro says it will look full from Monday night through Wednesday evening. Petro says it should look roughly 17% bigger and 30% brighter than 2026's smallest full moon, enough that regular moon-watchers should notice.

Johns Hopkins professor Kevin Lewis suggests looking just after sunset, when the moon sits low and makes a striking sight. The Old Farmer's Almanac says December's cold moon on Dec. 23 will be the biggest and brightest supermoon of 2026.

  • A stunning supermoon peaks this week. Here's what to know - ksl.com

item.title: Utah AG aims to jail Kalshi co-founders, arguing state will 'enforce its laws'
item.description:
Kalshi co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara have been ordered to report to the Salt Lake County Jail for booking on Dec. 5, facing 14 charges that include gambling promotion. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown says the prediction market app's founders will get no special treatment and had ample warning that their business is illegal in Utah.

"If anything, you can bet on Utah enforcing its laws," Brown said. Brown argued that Utah, which with Hawaii bans all forms of gambling, is well placed to act because its constitution forbids gambling "under any pretense".

item.title: These Utah ski resorts open this week
item.description:
More Utah ski areas are set to open after last week's storms piled up to 3 feet of snow in the mountains, joining Brian Head and Solitude, which opened earlier. Brighton opens Tuesday, Nov. 24, for its 90th season, and Snowbird is opening two days ahead of its planned date.

Park City Mountain, which has picked up 38 inches of new snow, will run lifts out of both of its base areas. Snowbird general manager Dave Fields said the mountain "is in great shape for this time of year" and the resort wants to get people skiing when conditions allow.

item.title: Utah gas prices drop sharply over past month as economist predicts additional decline
item.description:
Utah's average price for regular gas fell to $3.83 a gallon Monday from $4.70 a month earlier, according to AAA, and Salt Lake County averaged $3.56. BYU economist Christian vom Lehn said prices could keep falling into January but likely won't return to the roughly $3 of a year ago.

Vom Lehn pointed to lower seasonal demand and more oil shipping out of the Middle East. Driver Missy Austin said prices are still too high: "I can't wait until they're so low that we can go on a vacation."

item.title: Federal appeals court gives President Donald Trump a path to erasing hush money conviction
item.description:
A 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals panel on Monday revived President Donald Trump's bid to move his New York hush money case to federal court, reversing a lower-court ruling that kept it in state court. Should the case remain in federal court, Trump could argue that his 34-count conviction should be thrown out on presidential immunity grounds.

The panel told a federal judge to decide promptly whether the Manhattan federal court should keep the case, and the ruling begins a pause in Trump's parallel state court appeal. A Trump legal team spokesperson said the president "appreciates the 2nd Circuit's prompt and correct ruling," while the Manhattan District Attorney's Office declined to comment.

  • Federal appeals court gives President Donald Trump a path to erasing hush money conviction - ksl.com

item.title: 'Don't borrow just to spend more': Utah financial expert warns about holiday financing offers
item.description:
Utah Valley University financial planning professor Shane Stewart is cautioning holiday shoppers against using zero-percent financing to spend more, saying such deals are better suited to restructuring or paying down debt. A 2026 WalletHub study found 78% of store cards with introductory zero-percent offers use deferred interest, which can charge interest back to the purchase date if any balance remains at the deadline.

WalletHub analyst Chip Lupo said store-card interest is reaching "record rates of up to 33%," and that shoppers focused on a deal may simply "sign on the dotted line" without carefully reviewing the terms.

  • 'Don't borrow just to spend more': Utah financial expert warns about holiday financing offers - ksl.com

item.title: Look inside the Utah prison plate plant — producing record license plate options
item.description:
Every license plate on Utah roads is made by inmates at a plant inside the Utah State Correctional Facility, which averages about 2,800 plates a day, according to production lead Jeffery Hernandez. Drivers now have 75 plate options to choose from, the most the state has ever offered, and the limited edition America 250 design is currently the top seller.

Only 20 inmates qualify for the jobs, which require a record free of violence and discipline problems and build skills for life after parole. Print tech Brian Urban said the work beats "staying back in the section" and lets workers "do something productive" there.

item.title: Trump orders the Army not to detonate bomb-making chemicals in Iowa without court approval
item.description:
President Donald Trump on Monday ordered the military to hold off on detonating 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at an Iowa Army ammunition plant until a federal appeals court approves the plan. The Army, which had already moved the blast date three times amid health and environmental worries and was aiming for Wednesday, had no immediate comment.

Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand said Sunday that "No good options exist" because of earlier decisions, while Rodney Johnson, mayor of Middletown, where the plant sits, said it has to go forward "so we can move on with our lives."

item.title: Salt Lake Temple rededication date announced
item.description:
The First Presidency of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced Monday that the renovated Salt Lake Temple's rededication is set for Dec. 5, 2027. More tickets for the April-to-October 2027 open house will be released Tuesday through the Temple Square app and TempleSquare.org.

The first wave of open house reservations, 1 million in all, was claimed in under a day. The church leaders said the remodel and seismic retrofit are finished, and their letter said the temple will again let people take part in "sacred and eternal ordinances" for themselves and their ancestors.

item.title: Chinese neuroscientist at Princeton is held by ICE after detention at Washington airport
item.description:
ICE officers detained Eva Yi Xie, a Chinese doctoral student in neuroscience at Princeton, on Thursday at Reagan National Airport while she was heading back to New Jersey after a conference. The Department of Homeland Security says Xie overstayed a 2016 visa and will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

Her lawyer, Kerry Doyle, said Xie came to the U.S. with her family at 14 and has been waiting on an asylum application for years, but DHS says such an application "does not confer legal status." Graduate school dean Rodney Priestley called news of the detention "distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community" in a statement.

item.title: States sue Musk companies over flood of sexualized images made with AI chatbot Grok
item.description:
Democratic attorneys general in Virginia and Oregon sued several Elon Musk companies, including SpaceX and X, on Monday, alleging they launched the Grok chatbot without standard safeguards and fueled a flood of nonconsensual sexualized images. Virginia is seeking $2,500 for each willful violation of its consumer protection law plus a court order against further violations, and Oregon's separate suit makes a similar request.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in the suit that "weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature." SpaceX Super Intelligence, the SpaceX unit that developed Grok, called such content "abhorrent" and said it tightened protections once bad actors found ways to misuse the tool.

  • States sue Musk companies over flood of sexualized images made with AI chatbot Grok - ksl.com

item.title: Utah Community Credit Union strike $7M partnership with Southern Utah University
item.description:
Southern Utah University and Utah Community Credit Union have signed a multi-year, $7 million partnership, one of the largest sponsorship deals in the university's history. The money will put a UCCU branch with one-on-one financial coaching on campus and help pay for a football operations building and a digital billboard along I-15.

The deal also promises student jobs, and SUU President Mindy Benson said it reflects "a shared investment in our students' lives and long-term momentum" in a statement. The university said preparations for the branch and the new facilities will "begin soon."

item.title: Bill Clinton tells governors he hopes new political landscape can 'take some of the poison out'
item.description:
Former President Bill Clinton urged newly elected governors meeting in Park City to list concrete goals and work together on the country's biggest problems, including rebuilding trust. He spoke Thursday with Maryland Gov. Wes Moore at a National Governors Association forum attended by 33 new governors and 10 incumbents.

Clinton said he hoped the national mood could "take some of the poison out," while keeping healthy argument. He told them many won because voters thought they were "on the level" and in it for them.

item.title: Utah man wins 1st place for United States in The Great Wall of China Marathon
item.description:
Utah runner Michael Scott Peters placed fourth overall and first among Americans at The Great Wall of China Marathon, finishing in 4 hours and 50 minutes. He plans to run the Thanksgiving Point Half Marathon next and the Tokyo Marathon next year.

Peters, who signed up with only a month to prepare, described uneven, crumbling stairs made "extra slippery" by the race's first rain in 26 years. It was his 44th marathon and his first outside the country.

item.title: Anthropic's record IPO raises hopes for a charitable windfall that has nonprofits preparing to scale
item.description:
Anthropic's stock market debut at a record $1.5 trillion valuation has nonprofits preparing for a possible surge in donations from its founders and newly wealthy employees. The company plans to set aside 5% of its shares for a public benefit fund and its seven co-founders have pledged 80% of their equity, though many employees cannot sell or give away most of their stock before next spring.

GiveDirectly CEO Nick Allardice described "cautious optimism" about the preparations. Renaissance Philanthropy president Kumar Garg warned that putting philanthropic money to work is not automatic.

item.title: Murray mother of 6 seriously injured in hit-and-run
item.description:
Murray police have not identified the driver who struck Amanda Turnbow, a 37-year-old mother of six, as she rode her electric scooter near 6500 South and Cottonwood Street early Saturday and then left. Her family says she suffered a shattered spine, internal injuries and broken bones, and they are asking nearby businesses and residents to check surveillance footage.

Turnbow, a cook at P.F. Chang's, is the sole provider for her children and relied on the scooter to get to work. "She deserves better than what she got," said her sister Alisha Turnbow.

item.title: Delta Air Lines says issue that delayed flights nationwide has been resolved
item.description:
Delta Air Lines said it fixed a problem with its automated weight-and-balance system that forced manual workarounds Sunday and delayed flights across its network at the start of Thanksgiving travel week. More than half of Delta's flights were delayed and 6% canceled as of Sunday night, according to FlightAware, and passengers could still see lingering effects.

The issue caused an hourslong ground delay for Delta at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson, and the FAA said it was unrelated to its air traffic systems. A ramp worker told a pilot over the radio that crews were "manually counting bags" without the usual worksheet.

item.title: Lawyer: Father and daughter detained by ICE at Seattle airport were traveling to family baptism
item.description:
ICE officers detained a father and daughter on a Seattle-Tacoma International Airport jet bridge Saturday as they boarded a flight to a family baptism in California, according to their lawyer. ICE says both are from Mexico and overstayed their visas, and that the daughter threw hot coffee on officers; she could face a charge of assaulting a federal officer.

Lawyer Olia Catala said the pair are seeking asylum, have no criminal record and have lived in the U.S. since 2015, calling the arrest "just heartbreaking." Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called ICE's tactics "deeply un-American" and urged abolishing the agency.

item.title: Appeals court says federal law requiring accommodations for pregnant workers is unconstitutional
item.description:
The full 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled 9-8 that the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act is unconstitutional because most House members were not physically present when it passed by proxy vote in December 2022. Advocates say the ruling invalidates the law in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, and the group A Better Balance expects an appeal to the Supreme Court.

A Better Balance president Inimai Chettiar called the decision "legally unsound and short-sighted." The eight dissenting judges noted that no lawmaker raised a quorum objection when the $1.7 trillion funding bill passed.

item.title: Park City's Light the World Giving Machine helps those locally and internationally
item.description:
Park City unveiled its own Light the World Giving Machine on Saturday at the plaza east of The Market, where donors can buy gifts from $5 to $150 for seven local and international nonprofits. The machine is expected to stay open around the clock through Dec. 31, with all donations going directly to the charities.

Ballerina Farm's Hannah and Daniel Neeleman made the first gift. Project lead Karen Marriott said people want to feel "that spirit of giving" the machine offers.

item.title: What are digital license plates? Utah to consider a bill that would allow them
item.description:
Utah Senate Minority Whip Karen Kwan, D-Murray, is drafting a bill for the 2027 session that would let drivers use digital license plates, electronic displays that show the plate number and can update registration details. She previewed the concept Wednesday for the Transportation Interim Committee so members could weigh it before the session opens Jan. 19.

The bill would bar GPS tracking and the sale of drivers' data to outside vendors. Kwan said, "There's nothing stored on the license plates."

item.title: Ground beef by air: Delivery drones coming to a Walmart near you
item.description:
Alphabet-owned Wing expects to start drone deliveries from a Walmart store in the Salt Lake City area in early 2027, expanding a service it already operates in four other states. Shoppers within about 6 miles of a participating store could receive small orders in under five minutes through the Walmart or Wing apps.

Wing spokesperson Jessie Poole-Strang said the system can move 2-pound packages "without a 2-ton vehicle" and that ground beef is the most common order. Each parking-lot hub of charging pads still needs local permits.

item.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' sets record with $3.79B in first-day retail sales, Rockstar Games reports
item.description:
Rockstar Games said Grand Theft Auto VI brought in a record $3.79 billion in worldwide retail sales on its first day, based on company estimates. That far outpaces the $1 billion its predecessor took in over three days in 2013, and Rockstar also reported 32.5 million units sold before launch.

Founder Sam Houser said the company was "incredibly humbled" by players' response. Market research firm Sensor Tower had earlier put the game's revenue lower, at $2.36 billion.

item.title: US Army plans to invoke emergency provisions to detonate bomb-making chemicals in Iowa
item.description:
The U.S. Army plans to use emergency provisions to go ahead with detonating degraded, unstable lead azide in Middletown, Iowa, despite an appeals court order that put the permit on hold. Government lawyers argue colder weather raises the risk of an uncontrolled explosion, while environmental groups call the move an end run around the court.

Earthjustice attorney Thien Chau said the Army seemed focused on finding "a way to sidestep the judicial process" rather than on transparency. Residents in the region have been told to stay indoors, and an advisory says the blasts will release lead-containing particles.

item.title: Democrats clinch a historic House majority of at least 258 seats, the largest since 1992
item.description:
House Democrats have won at least 258 seats, their largest majority from a general election since 1992, after Chuck Hubbard's defeat of Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina pushed them to that mark Sunday. With the Senate also under Democratic control, the party plans a 100-day agenda on living costs, including reversing Medicaid cuts, alongside wide-ranging investigations of President Donald Trump.

Colorado Rep. Jason Crow said Democrats "should feel pressure" to deliver. Four House races remain undecided, and Republicans will hold at least 173 seats.

item.title: Marco Rubio shares how faith informs his work as 2028 presidential bid rumors mount
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the Federalist Society's National Lawyers Convention that Judeo-Christian beliefs about individual dignity underpin the American legal system, including the presumption of innocence. His remarks, later reshared by his Instagram and the State Department, come amid speculation over whether he will seek the presidency in 2028.

Asked how his religion shapes his work, Rubio said, "Attorney is what you do," adding, "Your faith is who you are."

item.title: Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the conflict began
item.description:
Reported attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz have reached their highest level since the U.S.-Iran war began in February, topping 30 in October with at least 22 so far in November, according to UKMTO data analyzed by CNN. Experts say Iran is losing leverage over the waterway as oil prices fall and could escalate further to force concessions from Washington.

Projectiles hit three tankers leaving the strait Friday and Saturday, and risk firm Marisks said Iranian involvement was "assessed as likely." Crisis Group analyst Hamidreza Azizi said markets' assumption that full-scale war is unlikely to return "could change quickly" if Iran intensifies the confrontation.

item.title: Davis County high school artists share stories through their work in art exhibit
item.description:
Davis County high schoolers displayed their work Thursday at the Davis Arts Council's annual student art competition and exhibit at the Davis Conference Center in Layton. Unlike most Utah student shows, it accepts any piece meeting minimum requirements, according to the council, and the art stays on view through Jan. 11.

First-place winner Carys Vandegrift, 17, said her oil painting was inspired by her mother and her recently deceased grandfather. "I was not expecting that at all," Vandegrift said of her awards.

item.title: Elder Rasband visits Mia Love's son on his mission
item.description:
Apostle Ronald A. Rasband of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints met with Elder Peyton Love, the missionary son of the late Utah Rep. Mia Love, to talk about his service and his mother's legacy. Rasband, whose New York missionaries taught Mia Love the gospel while he led the mission, told Peyton he knows his mother helped inspire his assignment to the Dominican Republic.

Peyton said his father, Jason Love, served under Rasband and trained the missionary "that baptized my mother." In the Dominican Republic, Peyton has taught and baptized a young Haitian man and his two sisters.

item.title: Macy's unveils 2026 Candy Window display in downtown Salt Lake
item.description:
Macy's at City Creek Center unveiled its 2026 Candy Window on Saturday, featuring candy ornaments built by five Salt Lake-area artists around the theme There's Magic Inside. Each ornament used hundreds of pounds of sweets, and the display is expected to stay up until Jan. 1.

Artist Jennifer Vesper, who has made nine ornaments over the years, built this year's as a bursting piñata spilling candy. "I love to do this every year with Macy's," she said.

item.title: Why this lawmaker wants to improve glass recycling in Utah
item.description:
Rep. Douglas Welton, R-Payson, previewed a 2027 bill that would create a restricted state account for grants and education to expand glass recycling, especially in rural areas that lack it. Legislators on an interim committee liked the idea but asked how parts like the education program would be funded and suggested making Inland Port Authority partnerships optional.

A 2025 study, ordered by an earlier bill from Welton and Sen. Derrin Owens, found nearly half of Utah counties had no glass recycling access. Glass dumped in a landfill "sits there forever and ever and ever and ever," Welton said.

item.title: Japanese Church of Christ celebrates historic roots in Salt Lake City
item.description:
The Japanese Church of Christ, one of the last buildings left from Salt Lake City's historic Japantown, has put the contents of a century-old time capsule recovered from its basement wall on display. Documents inside date the church's founding to October 1919, and Pastor Andrew Fleishman says the congregation dreams of expanding at its corner, though nothing is planned yet.

Fleishman says the church's bond with the Salt Lake Buddhist Temple down the street is "incredibly unique" and strengthened by the history the two buildings share. Trustee and former University of Utah historian Lorraine Crouse led the search that located the capsule.

item.title: Chair of Utah Democrats: 'We're still riding high'
item.description:
Utah Democratic Party Chair Brian King says the Nov. 3 election, which is expected to end the Republican supermajority in the Utah House, has energized his party more than anything since 1980. He predicts Republicans will struggle over the next two years because voters are unhappy with the country's direction under President Donald Trump.

King points to Blake Townsend's upset of longtime Republican Rep. Jim Dunnigan in House District 36 as a sign of the shift. King credits Trump with giving Democrats an "orange wind in our sails" and says, "We're still riding high."

item.title: Whether you're team plastic or wood, here's how to sanitize your cutting board
item.description:
An AP guide argues the wood-versus-plastic cutting board debate matters less than how a board is cleaned and cared for. Rutgers food scientist Donald Schaffner sanitizes boards after raw meat with boiling water, a dishwasher sanitize cycle or diluted bleach, because tap water is not hot enough to kill bacteria.

Vinegar and hydrogen peroxide are "not nearly as effective as bleach," Schaffner said. Good Housekeeping's Nicole Papantoniou says wood boards should be oiled and replaces boards that warp, crack or develop deep grooves.

item.title: Millions of American drivers are speeding. The environment could be paying the price
item.description:
A study of more than 120 million U.S. vehicle trips estimates that obeying posted speed limits could cut daily fuel use by an average of 6.7 million gallons and carbon dioxide emissions by 57,000 metric tons, saving $22 million. The trade-off would be just 54 seconds of added travel per driving day, with savings comparable to taking about 5.5 million cars off the road.

Driving 10 mph over the limit on a typical highway can boost fuel consumption and emissions as much as 21%, according to the study. Researcher Northrop said rushing through traffic is "just not worth it."

item.title: Daybreak Winter Village offers new ways to give back
item.description:
Winter Village at Downtown Daybreak in South Jordan has added a JustServe Giving Machine kiosk that matches visitors with volunteer projects, alongside the Light the World Giving Machine, where people buy donations such as meals, flu vaccines and shelter for those in need. Braxton Andersen of West Jordan, visiting with his wife, five children and extended family, said his kids favor the soccer ball donation and that the season is a time to remember Christ, who he said "would, of course, give and donate at this time". Organizers expect about 40,000 visitors to Holiday Lights at the Ballpark, and the village runs through Jan. 2, with the ice rink open through Feb. 15.

item.title: Little Mercury gets its first visitor in years as a pair of spacecraft loop into orbit
item.description:
The joint European-Japanese BepiColombo mission, a $2 billion pair of linked spacecraft launched in 2018, entered orbit around Mercury on Saturday after a roundabout journey that included flybys of Earth, Venus and Mercury itself and more than 6 billion miles of travel. It is only the third spacecraft to visit the planet and the first in over 10 years, following NASA's Mariner 10 in the 1970s and Messenger, which orbited from 2011 until crashing in 2015. The two craft will separate next month to study Mercury from different altitudes, and with temperatures there that can top 800 degrees, lead project scientist Geraint Jones called keeping them cool "a huge technical challenge in itself".

item.title: Holy Cross Hospital hosts community party to celebrate 50 years of serving others
item.description:
Holy Cross Hospital-Davis, which opened in Layton in 1976 and grew from 225 employees to nearly 800, celebrated its 50th anniversary Saturday with a free community party at the CommonSpirit Center in Farmington. Children tried out stethoscopes, practiced changing hospital bed sheets and operated the hospital's surgical robot, while vendors ran a teddy bear clinic that showed what to do if someone has a stroke or heart attack. "A lot has changed in 50 years," hospital President Kyle Brostrom said, but not "our passion for caring for our community."

item.title: Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight
item.description:
Masked ICE officers detained two people on a jet bridge as passengers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday, a scene the airline called "distressing" and said came with no advance notice. ICE said it was targeting Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, who it said overstayed his visa, and that Sofia Hernandez Mejia, who it said also overstayed a visa, threw hot coffee on officers; the AP reports she may be charged with assaulting a federal officer. Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called for abolishing ICE, whose tactics he called "deeply un-American", and said he believes the officers broke a March state law he signed restricting face coverings for law enforcement.

item.title: 2 visions of conservatism collide in deep-red Idaho
item.description:
After a Virginia-based PAC's mailer campaign helped hard-right challengers oust four moderate Republican incumbents around Twin Falls in 2024, former state Rep. Chenele Dixon, one of those defeated, joined other centrist Republicans in building a counteroffensive that unseated three of the four winners in this year's primaries, Mark Dee reports. In a state where Republicans will hold 80% of both legislative chambers, Boise State political scientist Jaclyn Kettler said a flip typically means switching "from one ideological faction to another"; in the Magic Valley, retiring Rep. Jack Nelsen said, votes against community college funding and water infrastructure money hurt the incumbents. The self-declared Gang of Eight was cut to three in the Nov. 3 midterm, but Kettler cautioned that results are mixed statewide, with hard-liners winning in northern Idaho.

item.title: AARP Utah to caregivers: 'You don't have to be perfect'
item.description:
Don Clawson, 80, who helps his 80-year-old husband with daily tasks like putting on his socks, said caregiver classes in Weber County have helped the couple greatly and taught him to share the load with family. The classes, where Weber Human Services helps cover care so caregivers can attend, included an AARP Utah session on burnout in which Darren Hotton told caregivers, "You don't have to be perfect." By AARP's count, Utah caregivers who pay their own way spend about $7,200 a year, and Weber Human Services' Angela Stout suggested concrete ways to help, such as bringing pizza or sitting with a loved one for two hours.

item.title: Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10%
item.description:
President Donald Trump told Fox News on Saturday he would work with the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress to cap credit card interest rates, a 2024 campaign promise he proposed in January as part of an affordability push but couldn't deliver amid industry pressure and little interest from fellow Republicans. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee, responded, "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money." The standard proposal would cap rates at 10%, well below the roughly 22.2% median rate in an August New York Fed survey, and researchers who studied the pledge estimated Americans would save about $100 billion in interest a year.

item.title: Annual turkey drive gathers 3,700 turkeys for Utah families
item.description:
The Frank Cordova Foundation will deliver turkeys Monday to 14 schools along the Wasatch Front, providing free birds for 3,700 families whose children attend Title I schools through a drive that began 27 years ago. It started when Frank Cordova, picking up his wife from the school where she worked, heard a child say the family couldn't afford a Thanksgiving turkey and drove to the store to buy them one. His son Gregorio Cordova, who has led the drive for five years, called it "my father's legacy" and said people can still donate throughout the year.

item.title: Nations agree to extend talks on AI killer robots but no firm commitment to rein them in
item.description:
A weeklong U.N. weapons conference in Geneva ended Saturday with countries agreeing only to "elaborate" a possible accord on lethal autonomous weapons by 2028, stopping short of the binding rules sought by Secretary-General António Guterres, who had set a 2026 deadline to launch negotiations. Activists said military powers such as Russia and the United States blocked tougher wording, with advocacy groups pointing largely at Russia, and Stop Killer Robots lamented a "watered-down mandate". Because the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons works by consensus, any one country can block a deal, and a proposal by seven countries including Brazil and Austria to begin negotiations fell short.

item.title: 'Connect us as humans': Springville art exhibit highlights research on isolation, social connection
item.description:
Co-created with BYU social connection researcher Julianne Holt-Lunstad, one of whose best-known findings is that lacking social connection can be as harmful as smoking 15 cigarettes a day, the Springville Museum of Art's exhibit In This Together features 22 artists chosen from about 400 proposals and runs from Wednesday through July 3, 2027. The show grew out of the museum adding connection to its mission statement, director Emily Larsen said, adding that one main reason art exists is "to connect us as humans". Among the artists is high school teacher Ryan Moffett, whose sculpture Apart we fall apart, inspired by a Mumford and Sons lyric, traces a couple drifting apart until one figure is left alone and broken.

item.title: Speaker Johnson pleads with House Republicans to return to work after bruising midterm losses
item.description:
After low attendance forced House GOP leaders to cancel votes this week, with 21 Republicans, at least 12 of them not returning next Congress, missing Thursday morning votes, Speaker Mike Johnson sent colleagues a letter Friday pleading with them to come back after Thanksgiving. With 12 work days left before Democrats take control of both chambers in January, Johnson wants to pass government funding, the National Defense Authorization Act and a Senate-passed permitting reform bill, which would otherwise have to clear the Senate again. He wrote that "barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here" for the rest of the term.

item.title: 6 charged in alleged 'prostitution ring' that operated through Utah massage parlors
item.description:
A federal indictment filed Nov. 18 accuses six people, including Springville's Yongzhen Yang, described by prosecutors as the "leader" of the scheme, of conspiring to commit human trafficking and money laundering and of sex trafficking by force or coercion over an alleged prostitution ring run through massage parlors from Orem to Ogden. Prosecutors allege at least three victims were required to live at the parlors, rotated among them and taken to five other states, and pushed to offer sex under threat of not being paid; a worker at a Woods Cross parlor told an undercover agent she "won't earn a single penny" unless customers paid for sex, court documents say. Yang was the registered agent for 10 Utah massage parlors between 2016 and 2026 and sold nine of them to others, including co-defendants Kristian Walker Bryant and Jia Ming Zhou, the complaint says.

item.title: Route 66 barbershop builds community through license plate stories
item.description:
Francisco Alcantar has covered the walls of his Albuquerque barbershop on Route 66 with about 400 license plates from around the world, a collection that began with a plate from his own 1984 Chevy and grew as customers brought back or mailed in plates from their travels. He started it for tourists, but local regulars embraced it, and Alcantar, who has cut hair on the historic road for more than two decades, credits them: "The shop has put itself together." He estimates it would take roughly 500 more plates to fill the shop.

item.description:
Amid a disparity documented by a 2023 state task force, which found American Indian and Alaska Native residents make up 1.6% of Utah's population but 5% of its murder victims, Rep. Angela Romero, a Salt Lake City Democrat, will pursue a 2027 bill directing the Department of Public Safety's POST division to create law enforcement training on missing person investigations, with a component on missing and murdered Indigenous people. Romero, an enrolled Shoshone-Bannock member who said the issue has touched her own family, said DPS asked for a broader scope to address a gap in how officers learn to handle missing person cases. If passed, the voluntary training would be offered by Dec. 1, 2027, and MMIR Utah's Tammy Dee Platero noted the issue isn't only rural, with roughly 50,000 American Indian and Alaska Native people on the Wasatch Front.

item.title: 'A place to remember': Memorial in Davis County dedicated to victims of Agent Orange in Vietnam
item.description:
A large orange and black monument dedicated Friday at Sunset City Veterans Memorial Park honors Vietnam veterans harmed by Agent Orange, along with those exposed to burn pits and other toxins in later Gulf and Afghanistan operations; Larry Kerr, who leads the Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation behind it, believes it is the largest such memorial in the country. Kerr, an Air Force veteran recently diagnosed with cancer, and other speakers hope it will teach younger generations, and Hannah Smalling, whose father is battling Agent Orange's effects, said she hopes it helps the next generation understand "that freedom has a human cost". Retired Army colonel Marlene Summers lamented that the veterans had to find the resources themselves, telling them, "My apologies you had to do that for yourself."

item.description:
Mexico's military captured Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, the alleged Los Mazatlecos cartel leader known as "El Chapo Isidro" and listed among the FBI's 10 most wanted with a $5 million reward offered for information leading to his arrest, in a Friday operation in Sinaloa that, according to the defense ministry, had U.S. help and drew attacks with gunfire and explosives. Fans and players fled a baseball game at Kuroda Park stadium amid gunfire, and a local resident told CNN that armed individuals had taken over private hospitals while businesses were being set on fire. Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch said the group's second-in-command and its alleged financial operator were also arrested.

item.description:
Morris Mullins, who was 17 when he killed 78-year-old Amy Davis in Richfield in 2001 and later pleaded guilty to aggravated murder, will be resentenced after the U.S. Supreme Court declined in October to review a Utah Supreme Court ruling that his life-without-parole sentence was unconstitutional. The state court's majority pointed to the original judge's stated "hope" that Mullins might change, finding a juvenile life-without-parole sentence "incompatible with a suggestion that Mullins could change." At a hearing Tuesday, Mullins, now 43 and held in the Sevier County Jail, sought a transfer the judge doubted was possible, and Judge Robert Van Dyke appointed a local public defender and set a Dec. 15 status conference before any new sentencing date.

item.description:
A blood sample Box Elder County Sheriff Kevin Potter gave voluntarily two hours after an Oct. 27 Ogden crash measured .065, above Utah's .05 limit, and charges say his level at the time of the crash "was likely higher". Potter has been arrested and charged with second-degree felony automobile homicide in the death of 22-year-old motorcyclist Katie Sue Ruth Huggins, who the charges say had the right-of-way; Ogden Police Capt. item.title: Winter weather creates challenges for Utah drivers
item.description:
Utah drivers are crashing more often than at any earlier point this season as snow, rain and cold settle in, and UDOT spokesman Nic Naylor attributed the spike to drivers adjusting, saying "we're not used to this". On Friday, a crash involving a semi closed US-40 for a time and left one person in critical condition, the Utah Highway Patrol said, while canyon regular John Gaspar described the Cottonwood Canyons as "usually a zoo" full of vehicles that should not be heading up there. Naylor said snowplow operators, UDOT's traffic operations center and its meteorologist are coordinating their response, and drivers are urged to slow down, leave extra room and check conditions on the UDOT Traffic website or app.

item.description:
Spanish Fork police say a van struck 25-year-old Alan Zelaya as he walked with his brother and mother on Nov. 4 and kept going; investigators later tracked the vehicle down with neighborhood surveillance video, and Maria Del Rocio Morales Ruvalcaba, 51, of Sanpete County now faces a charge of leaving the scene of a crash that caused serious injury; investigators said she told police she thought she had struck a bicycle. Brother Ricky Zelaya, who wrapped his work jacket around Alan's bleeding head, said Alan suffered multiple fractures, among them injuries to his head and pelvis; Alan, who was in a coma after the crash, has since regained consciousness. The Spanish Fork Culver's, where Ricky is a shift manager, is holding a Nov. 30 fundraiser from 5 to 8 p.m., and organizers say all proceeds from food sold that evening will go toward Alan's recovery costs.

item.title: Resorts optimistic about ski season ahead of 2026 Thanksgiving weekend
item.description:
Back-to-back storms have Utah resorts upbeat heading into Thanksgiving week, with Alta spokesperson Lexi Dowdall saying the resort already has a 60-inch base before its planned Wednesday opening, a sharp turn from 2025, when scant early snow pushed Alta's opening back 16 days and the season totaled 321 inches against a typical 550. Ski Utah lists Brighton opening the Tuesday before the holiday and Snowbird and Snowbasin expected on Black Friday, and Ski Utah's Alison Palmintere pointed to the "Super El Niño" pattern as a good sign for snowfall. Dowdall also highlighted a new east wing at Alta's Albion Lodge with 4,000 more square feet of dining space, while reminding skiers that the best part of Alta's season is "in March and April when the snow depth is incredibly deep."

Deputies arrested Emery County resident Tabitha Elizabeth Bringhurst, 44, at her home, where they found a black Ford Explorer with marks that appeared to show something sliding down its driver's side, along with the husband of the woman she is accused of hitting. The Cincinnati Zoo said Friday that a necropsy found the hat Fiona swallowed had lodged in the middle of her small intestine, 25 feet beyond her final stomach compartment, so far along that no supportive care could have saved the 9-year-old hippo. "No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success," said Mike Wenninger, the zoo's director of animal health, who added that surgery was impossible given the hat's location and hippo anatomy. Fans have left flowers and crayon-written notes on a hippo statue at the zoo, and the Field Museum in Chicago confirmed it received the remains of a Cincinnati Zoo hippo that died in 1923 after a boy threw a rubber ball into its mouth.

item.description:

The county had generated the voice with an ElevenLabs tool trained on snippets of a police interview, hoping to present Yost's 1985 preliminary hearing testimony, which survives only as a transcript; after an August hearing where Lovell's defense brought two experts to oppose it, ElevenLabs refused to license its software for the purpose. Chief Criminal Deputy Attorney Branden Miles told the judge the county has been unable to find another provider willing to help; prosecutors have previously had human proxies read Yost's words, and the re-sentencing is scheduled for September 2027.

item.description:
Liberty Village, a 32-acre Hurricane site founded by Lex Howard in 2022 to recreate 18th-century American landmarks as to-scale replicas, is developing a Future Native Village exhibit with Indigenous tribal members, among them Betsy "Red Ant" LaFontaine of the Navajo Nation; no completion date has been set. item.title: UHSAA takes first step toward 2027-29 realignment with debut of Competitive Realignment Index
item.description:
Utah High School Activities Association trustees opened the 2027-29 realignment Thursday by finalizing a new Competitive Realignment Index, keeping general sports at 77% enrollment, 13% socioeconomic data and 10% performance while moving football from a provisional 85-8-7 draft to a 65-13-22 split that more than triples the weight of three years of on-field results. After reviewing index scores with school names hidden, the board set initial class sizes, growing 6A from its current 17 teams to 22 for 11-man football and 21 for general sports. Schools may no longer appeal to drop a class over competitive struggles, only over geography and travel, and the board reconvenes Dec. 1 ahead of final approval Dec. 17, with competition under the new alignment beginning in August 2027.

item.title: Nasdaq wipes out gains for the year as Anthropic IPO fails to quell AI nerves
item.description:
A worsening tech sell-off erased the Nasdaq's gains for the year Friday with a 5.28% drop, while the S&P 500 fell 3.7% for a seventh straight losing day, its longest such streak since February 2020, and both it and the Dow closed in correction. Anthropic's newly public shares slid 9% to $88.30, just above the $83 IPO price, and Nvidia finished its worst week since October 2008 down 22.7%, as investors weighed returns on AI spending, how newly elected Democratic governors might affect the data center buildout, and Nvidia's role after CEO Jensen Huang resigned. Some strategists think the fears may be overblown: JPMorgan Asset Management's David Kelly likened the slump to "a mild cold" that he expects to pass within a week or two, and CFRA's Arun Sundaram said "the fundamentals don't really justify all this selling".

item.description:
Officers who searched the Pleasant Grove home of Russell Dillon Woodard, 41, on Tuesday seized numerous devices, including one the affidavit says was hidden between his mattress and box spring, and investigators say they are "concerned there are other victims yet to be uncovered". Woodard faces 18 felony charges in 4th District Court, among them 10 first-degree aggravated sexual exploitation counts. A police affidavit alleges he coached a 14-year-old West Virginia girl into producing explicit photos while leading her to believe he was also a minor, though he was about 40 at the time; Pittsburgh FBI agents had alerted local police that one of multiple adult men allegedly abusing the girl online appeared to live in Pleasant Grove.

item.title: Utah picks new water agent as battle over Colorado River continues
item.description:
Gov. Spencer Cox has named Zach Renstrom, general manager of the Washington County Water Conservancy District, as Utah's water agent, a post lawmakers created in 2024 to seek supplies from beyond the state's borders and previously held by Joel Ferry, who left as natural resources commissioner in August. Senate President Stuart Adams, who sponsored the bill creating the role, backed the choice, crediting Renstrom with a "practical understanding" of turning big water plans into finished projects. The appointment follows the Colorado River Basin states' failure to agree on managing Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which led to a federal 10-year plan that Nevada and Arizona have sued over because of mandatory cuts for Lower Basin states.

item.title: Fiona's death gives parents a chance to teach kids about grief — and life
item.description:
For many children, the death of Fiona, the 9-year-old Cincinnati Zoo hippo who died Thursday after swallowing a knit hat, may be their first loss of an animal they loved, and psychologists and grief specialists say it can give parents an opening to talk about death. Experts advise plain, age-appropriate explanations that Fiona is not coming back, warning that euphemisms such as "went to sleep" can confuse or scare young kids, and say parents can share their own sadness and return to the subject over time. Samantha Haines of St. Petersburg, Florida, said she and her hippo-loving 10-year-old cried together for about 20 minutes, while a Wisconsin mother said her 8-year-old took comfort in picturing Fiona in heaven with the family dog.

item.title: (Not) up in the air: Travelers' trepidations spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups abound
item.description:
As Thanksgiving travel week gets underway, some fliers are uneasy after last week's rare nationwide ground stop, the longest since 9/11, a separate airline outage and a string of other tech failures, though UNLV aviation historian Dan Bubb said grumbling travelers "are still going to do it." The bigger pain may be price: Hopper estimated in late October that roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas are up 39% and 40% from a year ago, the highest holiday fares in a decade, with some increases tied to jet fuel costs linked to the war in Iran. Miami frequent flier Michelle Jolene, who says delays no longer rattle her, covered her daughter's flight home from Washington, D.C., with roughly 8,500 American Airlines miles earned by buying 10 boxes of toilet paper through the airline's shopping portal.

item.title: UK and EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, pledging to rebuild ties after Brexit
item.description:
At a Brussels summit Friday, Britain and the EU sealed agreements that drop checks on farm and food trade, connect the two emissions trading systems and open up to three years of residence and work for 100,000 young adults in each direction, while giving themselves six months to settle tuition fees for each other's students. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has said rejoining the bloc should remain an option though it is far from imminent, called the package a "historic moment" and estimated it could add 0.5% to Britain's economy. Brexit supporters object that Britain must accept EU rules it has no hand in setting, and Nigel Farage, who leads Reform UK, told the BBC the Brexit debate "has just started again".

item.title: European troops from 11 countries hold a drill in Poland for a potential postwar Ukraine mission
item.description:
About 2,800 personnel from nine European countries, with Poland handling logistics and Turkey taking part remotely from Istanbul, are in a two-week exercise at Poland's Nowa Deba training ground that for the first time tests whether the France- and U.K.-led Coalition of the Willing could deploy to Ukraine after the war. If sent once a ceasefire holds, the force would help rebuild Ukraine's military, provide the reassurance needed to reopen its airspace and clear Black Sea mines, its commander has said, though it would have no peacekeeping role, and U.K. Brig. Campbell Close said, "We are a defensive force." The drill overlapped with a Russian missile crash about 47 miles away that Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called likely an intentional provocation, and Putin warned last year that any foreign troops in Ukraine would be "legitimate targets."

item.title: UN climate talks slammed by activists, leaders as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft agreement
item.description:
The draft final agreement at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, never mentions fossil fuels, setting off an uproar among activists and national leaders on Friday, the last scheduled day, though negotiators expect talks to spill into Saturday. Its main electrification goal, lifting electricity's share of global energy use from about 21% to 35% by 2035, doesn't specify renewable power, and a fund for climate-ravaged nations would be tripled with no dollar amount, while summit overseer Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, argued the electrification push implies a move away from fossil fuels. Panama threatened to "formally object" absent changes such as an oil production cap, and its environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, called the summits "an exercise in hypocrisy and futility".

item.title: Poland says a Russian missile that crashed in its territory was a provocation
item.description:
A Russian Kh-101 missile came down in Poland about 37 miles from the Ukrainian border Friday, apparently in a wooded area and with no immediate reports of injuries or damage, during an overnight Russian barrage of 400-plus drones and more than 110 missiles that Zelenskyy said killed at least eight civilians in Ukraine. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the crash appeared to be "an intentional provocation" timed to European military exercises under way in Poland, and NATO chief Mark Rutte called it a "grave violation" of Polish airspace. The strikes came hours after Putin vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian attacks on a bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia, and a Ukrainian deputy energy minister said hits on the power grid forced the country's three operating nuclear plants to cut output.

item.title: Mamdani sets plan to close NYC's notorious Rikers Island jail
item.description:
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Friday laid out a plan to shut the Rikers Island jail complex by 2032, well past a 2027 legal deadline the city is all but certain to miss, by cutting the number of people held there from more than 6,500 to around 4,500. The approach relies on new diversion and supervised release programs, expanded housing and social services, a restored online bail payment option and fewer case delays, with people shifted to borough jails expected to open from 2029 in Brooklyn through 2032 in Manhattan. Violence and overcrowding at Rikers had prompted a federal judge to appoint an outside manager, and in announcing the plan Mamdani said, "It is time to finally close Rikers Island".

item.title: Woman who survived hundreds-foot fall on Mount Timpanogos credits rescuers for saving her life
item.description:
Utah schoolteacher Amber Baumgartner is recovering from a broken neck, a broken elbow and other injuries after slipping on Oct. 26 while descending Mount Timpanogos and sliding hundreds of feet down a snowy slope to a small ledge, where she held herself in place for over an hour. With 911 calls dropping, her hiking group reached Utah County Sheriff's Office Search and Rescue by text, and its airplane pilot spotted her and coordinated with a Utah Department of Public Safety helicopter crew to reach her. Friend Josh Dunn said that when she asked a rescuer whether she would fall, he answered something like "No, I've got you," and friends have started a GoFundMe for her medical costs.

item.title: 'These kids deserve better': Mother speaks out after son's unlawful school seclusions
item.description:
A mother identified only as Lori told the KSL Investigators that her autistic 6-year-old son, Gunner, was secluded twice in kindergarten at the Davis School District's Orchard Elementary months after a 2025 law banned the practice for kindergartners, and that he has since grown scared of school and been secluded several more times in first grade. The district declined an interview, citing federal student privacy law and saying seclusion is a last resort, while state data show 1,565 seclusion incidents in 2025-26, up 37%, a rise state board coordinator Krisanne Lewis said is hard to read given increased scrutiny and policy and definition changes. Nate Crippes of the Disability Law Center said "Clearly our system is not working," and 15 state compliance letters obtained by KSL describe untrained staff, seclusions past the 30-minute limit and another secluded kindergartner.

item.title: Lehi family pays it forward after contractors donate garage remodel in son's memory
item.description:
After 20-year-old Dominic Millward, who loved fixing cars, died last month after drinking an unknown substance, JD Hepworth of Nova Concrete Coatings showed up at the family's Lehi home to bid an epoxy garage floor his mother had forgotten requesting, then rallied The Coating House, other suppliers and contractors, and sign company Notatek to remodel the garage in his memory for free. Mary Millward said sorting her son's tools with his friends was "very healing" and that she and her husband are putting memorial funds toward the medical debt of a young mother who had posted online looking for odd jobs and came to help clear the space. She said her next step is to keep helping others and "just keep doing good."

item.title: Salt Lake County 'Giving Tree' brings hope to older adults this holiday season
item.description:
Many tags on Salt Lake County Aging and Adult Services' Giving Tree, where donors pick an older adult's first name, age and wish list, are asking for basics this year, such as grocery and gas gift cards, blankets and walking sneakers. The agency's Emma Furman tied that to high gas and grocery prices, noting that Meals on Wheels, which supplied most recipients, has seen enrollment rise 28% this year, and said the goal is to fulfill wishes for 300 seniors. Gifts are due Nov. 30 at the county government center for volunteers to deliver in December, and Lea Robledo of the Liberty Senior Center said a warm meal for isolated seniors "changes their whole day."

item.title: Utah drivers can check canyon traction-law readiness with new UDOT quiz
item.description:
With snow piling up in the Wasatch Mountains, UDOT spokesperson Nic Naylor is urging Cottonwood Canyons visitors to take the agency's online traction law quiz, which helps drivers confirm their tires carry the M+S or three-peak mountain snowflake marking and have at least 5/32 of an inch of tread. Drivers can have their tread checked for free at locations listed on UDOT's website and get this year's new sticker, which Naylor said lets enforcers see a car's tires have been checked so it can "get up the canyon a little faster." Naylor said drivers should "prepare for and plan before you even hit the road," and warned that even rain raises the risk of hydroplaning.

item.title: Senate approves bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs
item.description:
The Senate voted 62-33 Thursday to pass a bipartisan overhaul meant to speed permitting for power plants, transmission lines and other energy projects and make data centers pay for the energy they use, sending it to the House, which passed a narrower, industry-friendly version last year. Negotiated by Republicans Shelley Moore Capito and Utah's Mike Lee with Democrats Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse, the bill drew 15 Democratic votes plus backing from Trump and industry groups, and Lee said it would make it "easier to build in America again". Environmental groups, tribal leaders and Democrats including Jeff Merkley and Maria Cantwell objected to limits on judicial review and changes to laws such as NEPA, with Jen Duggan of the Environmental Integrity Project calling it "a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America".

item.description:
Utah State University's Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water and Air delivered its annual report to the governor and Legislature, adding a new section on how lawmakers can handle data centers' demands on water and energy, while flagging the Great Salt Lake and noting that air quality keeps improving despite growth in population and power production. Institute executive director Anna McEntire said a lack of spring snow made 2026 "a rough year" of drought, wildfire and strain on farmers, and urged more precise use of water if winter stays dry. Newly elected state Rep. Patrick Belmont, a USU professor, said the lake "is worse off now than it was seven years ago" and that lawmakers should check whether spending is actually getting water to it.

Michelle Hill was hit with a $224 no-show penalty for a third room she had reserved through Booking.com at St. George's Coronada Inn & Suites over Easter weekend, even though the hotel couldn't find that reservation when her family arrived and she spent the stay in the other two rooms. Hill said the hotel first agreed she was owed a refund but later claimed she had initiated the cancellation; after Get Gephardt reached out, Booking.com did not respond, but an attorney for the hotel said "upper management agreed" she should get a full refund and asked the hotel to send her a check directly, and Hill got her money back. The KSL Investigators note that booking through a third-party travel site can save money but complicates matters when something goes wrong.

item.description:
Florida executed Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, on Thursday for the 1991 strangling of Michael and Susan MacIvor and the death of their unborn child in the Florida Keys, its 20th execution of 2026, a state record that tops the 19 carried out in 2025 under Gov. Ron DeSantis. Overton, linked to the crime by a DNA sample taken after an unrelated 1996 burglary arrest, maintained his innocence to the end, saying "I never killed anyone." Texas was set to execute Reinaldo Dennes, 70, about an hour later for the 1996 killing of Houston diamond dealer Janos Szucs during a $3.6-million heist, a pairing that spotlights the aging of the U.S. death row population.

Association President Sandy Webster said the reward, posted on signs for about 15 years after a string of sheep and cattle were shot and abandoned along the road, has not drawn a single lead, and the Iron County Sheriff's Office asks anyone with information to call Detective McIntyre at 435-867-7500. item.description:
Marriner Richards, a 19-year-old Marine from Syracuse, Utah, stationed at the Twentynine Palms Marine Corps base, has been missing since walking out of the Tortoise Rock Casino in Twentynine Palms, California, on Nov. 7, according to the San Bernardino County Sheriff's Office. Jenny Smith of the sheriff's office said deputies and detectives have canvassed nearby residents and businesses and searched neighboring Joshua Tree National Park with off-road vehicles and aircraft. His father, Brock Richards, said more than 40 locals turned out to search one day and 20 the next, and members of the family's church congregation and neighborhood were driving down from Utah to join more searches.

item.title: Sen. Curtis: Pay Utah's federal workers legit wages — or wave bye-bye to talent
item.description:
Utah Sen. John Curtis on Thursday introduced the Locality Pay Fairness and Improvement Act, which would rework how federal locality pay is calculated to weigh local housing costs, blue-collar wages and labor market conditions, after hearing concerns from federal workers at places like Hill Air Force Base that most Utah employees get the same adjustment as those in cheaper labor markets. The bill calls for an independent study, a multi-year research program and a pilot program, with Curtis saying Utah stakeholders are "anxious to be part of that pilot program" and warning that if federal workers "can't afford that house payment, we can't keep them." A similar amendment to the defense authorization bill failed last year after the American Federation of Government Employees opposed it, reportedly over fears the Trump administration would use it to cut pay, though Curtis said a union executive has since apologized.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints donated the land, Ivory Innovations and the Call to Action Foundation partnered on the project, and Elder John A. item.description:
The Justice Department on Thursday asked the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to declare moot its suit, filed at President Donald Trump's direction, to block certification of Democrat Mary Peltola's win in Alaska's U.S. Senate race over a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot, while also asking the court to vacate the lower court's dismissal. Peltola won an outright majority, Democrats' ninth Senate pickup, and the margin exceeded the votes cast for the second Sullivan, a retired Petersburg schoolteacher whom documents reported by The New York Times appeared to tie to recruiting by Peltola's campaign, which both deny. Alaska's Republican-led state government had called the administration's move legally "meritless"; it is the second high-profile election case the department has moved to drop since Nov. 3, after one targeting roughly 20,000 California ballots.

Jeremy Jack Hall, 44, of Hooper faces 41 felony counts filed Monday by Weber County prosecutors, the most serious being an aggravated sexual exploitation charge alleging that in 2024 he made abuse material depicting a young girl, apparently in a church classroom. Charging documents say Roy police, acting on a tip, found sexually explicit videos of children plus 27 more recordings of young girls in a cloud account, and that Hall, who appeared to serve as a teacher or youth leader for children ages 8 to 10, "admitted to secretly recording the juveniles" while acting as their teacher. The remaining charges are 19 exploitation counts for possessing abuse material and 21 voyeurism counts tied mostly to late 2025 and 2026; Hall is jailed ahead of a Dec. 3 court date.

Kim Ziebarth, a former interim president and vice president at Davis Technical College, will take over as president of Tooele Technical College on Jan. 1, 2027, after the state board of education voted unanimously Thursday to appoint her. Ziebarth has also been the Utah System of Higher Education's associate commissioner for technical education and a senior adviser to Commissioner Geoffrey Landward, and has held national roles with the Council on Occupational Education and the National Technical Honor Society. item.description:

item.title: The world is experiencing 'GTA VI' together — players and spectators alike
item.description:
Thursday's global launch of Grand Theft Auto VI turned a mostly solitary game into a shared event, with people spending more than 132 million hours watching streams across Twitch, YouTube and Kick on release day and nearly 8 million watching at once at one point, according to Streams Charts. The game has already made an estimated $1.8 billion; Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, citing its 99 out of 100 Metacritic score, called it "a massive creative achievement" for Rockstar, and everyone from the Miami Heat to Uber Eats to the Interior Department joined in the hype. item.title: Aerial reseeding operations taking place on Cottonwood Fire burn scar
item.description:
State wildlife and forestry agencies and contractor Hammond Helicopter are flying close to 500 airplane loads of seed out of the Junction airport to reseed about 56,000 acres of the roughly 97,000-acre Cottonwood Fire burn scar between Beaver and Piute counties with some 600,000 pounds of grasses, forbs and shrubs. Bare, burned slopes have already sent mud and debris into communities below and across U.S. 89 and I-15, and the new growth is meant to anchor soil while feeding deer and elk; "The faster we can get roots in the soil to hold that soil up on the mountain, the better," said the Division of Wildlife Resources' Gary Bezzant. The seed will sit dormant in the snow until melt carries it into the soil, and while success hinges on precipitation, forester Nicholas Dastrup said "great soil moisture right now" has crews hopeful.

item.title: 13 men charged in train-heist ring that netted $22M in cargo from major retailers
item.description:
A federal indictment unsealed Thursday in Los Angeles charges 13 men with conspiracy and theft of interstate railroad cargo, alleging they stole more than $22 million in goods such as Nike sneakers, Crocs and power tools from more than three dozen trains carrying imports from the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. The indictment alleges the group disabled trains at planned spots by busting the brakes, moved the merchandise onto trucks and sold it to an unnamed company for resale, while the men posted photos of themselves with cash and stolen goods in group chats. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli called the scale of the theft "staggering"; two of the men also face charges of violence against railroad carriers, and convictions could bring five to 20 years in federal prison.

item.title: Anthropic surges in market debut after biggest IPO on record, despite fears that AI is running amok
item.description:
Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, closed up 17% at $97.17 in its first day of trading Thursday after an IPO that overtook SpaceX as the largest ever, at one point topping $2 trillion in value despite worries about an AI bubble, the recent ouster of Nvidia's CEO and a possible crackdown next year by a Democratic-led Congress. The sale of 980 million shares raised $81 billion, and a planned $26 billion private sale was set to bring the total to $107 billion, giving the company, which carries $6.2 billion in debt, is unprofitable under standard accounting rules and has committed to $900 billion in computing and infrastructure spending, room to expand without borrowing more. CEO Dario Amodei pitched the company as proof that it's possible to make "the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company," while analyst Dan Ives called the debut "a big win for the tech sector".

item.title: How renowned artist plans to bring 'love' to Salt Lake City's Fleet Block
item.description:
Salt Lake City Arts Council officials said Thursday that New York artist Kenseth Armstead, chosen from 175 applicants, will create 2 Gather, a 20-foot-tall, 56-foot-wide polished aluminum sculpture spelling the word love in English, Spanish, Shoshoni, Nahuatl and Twi for the former city vehicle fleet parcel known as the Fleet Block. The council wanted a piece that carried the social justice spirit of the 29 murals of people killed by police that covered the site's walls until redevelopment began last year, and Gina Thayne, whose nephew was among those honored, wrote that "our murals were all about love, in so many different languages" in response to Armstead's video about the design. Armstead said of the project's call for artists that they were "asking for care," and the sculpture is expected to be installed by late 2028 or early 2029 in an open space funded with $6 million from the 2022 parks bond and $2 million from a Bezos Earth Fund grant.

item.title: St. George cancer center expansion brings specialized care closer to home
item.description:
Intermountain Health expanded the cancer center at St. George Regional Hospital in September, adding room for more infusion treatments, expanded palliative care and closer teamwork between specialists and support staff, and it has added a neuro-oncologist while recruiting more specialists. Oncologist Dr. Derrick Haslem said some specialized treatments may still require travel to larger hospitals, but consultations, preparation and follow-up can be handled locally, and patients kept close to home will be "so much better off physically, mentally and emotionally". For Pine Valley's Dana Rowley, whose multiple myeloma care has mostly been in St. George but required a trip to Salt Lake City for a stem cell transplant, the expansion hasn't changed his treatment yet, though his wife, Glenda, hopes it will spare other families from traveling as far.

item.title: Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo has died, days after ingesting a visitor's hat
item.description:
Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo hippo who became a worldwide sensation after surviving a premature birth in 2017, died Thursday of complications from swallowing a knit hat that a ceiling fan caught and flung into her enclosure after a visitor tossed it in the air about 11 days earlier. Specialists told the zoo surgery wasn't an option for a full-grown hippo, so the care team kept her hydrated, sedated her twice for exams and even borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm in hopes the shaking would move the hat along, but the zoo said it was "ultimately too much to overcome". Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval called Fiona "a symbol of perseverance and joy in Cincinnati"; zoos have warned for years about objects tossed or blown into animal habitats.
