item.title: Salt Lake Masonic Temple still open after nearly a century in Utah
item.description:
Nearly a century after its cornerstone was laid in 1926, Salt Lake City's Masonic Temple on South Temple, the fifth-largest in the country, is open to the public through year-round tours run by Preservation Utah, with a centennial ceremony set for Nov. 21. Visitors can see lodge rooms themed on American colonial, Egyptian and North African architecture, a theater whose ceiling shows the 1920s night sky, and Utah's second-oldest working elevator, while first-floor offices now house providers of free dental, vision and surgical care for children. Temple worker Ashlee Child began selling $10 tours at city markets to help pay for upkeep as attendance dwindled, and recalled that on her first try she "almost did $1,000 in one day".

item.description:
A Copa Airlines Boeing 737 clipped a UPS Boeing 767's nose with its wingtip as both taxied at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, leaving two people with minor injuries treated at the scene, a day after a nationwide FAA ground stop snarled travel. The FAA said controllers had told the UPS crew to yield to the Copa jet, and on air traffic audio the UPS pilot acknowledged, "we went too far," while the Copa pilot reported apparently losing the left wingtip. All 166 passengers and six crew members got off the Copa plane, which had arrived from Panama City, and the FAA is investigating.

item.title: Europe scrambles to respond to wave of bomb threats disrupting transport, media and schools
item.description:
A wave of emailed bomb threats, all false so far, has disrupted more than 50 flights, broadcasters, at least one cruise ship and thousands of schools across Europe, and Chatham House analyst Grégoire Roos told CNN each country is responding with "its own toolbox and standards" instead of a shared threat-assessment framework. Wizz Air CEO József Váradi has pressed European Commission officials for coordinated procedures, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni proposed that schools not be evacuated over a mass email without concrete evidence after some 6,300 Italian schools were targeted Wednesday, and Heathrow and Birmingham airports stayed open after judging threats not credible. Some suspect a hybrid-warfare campaign, but French President Emmanuel Macron said there is not yet enough evidence to attribute the threats, and cybersecurity firms found many came from hijacked webmail accounts.

item.title: Logan man who kidnapped child, requested ransom given less than a year in jail
item.description:
A Logan man charged with kidnapping an 11-month-old and demanding $6,000 for the infant's return was sentenced to 364 days in jail, with credit for 105 days served but no "good time" credit, after a plea deal dismissed the kidnapping counts. Renan Alberto Alvarez, 50, pleaded guilty to aggravated assault, domestic violence in the presence of a child, property damage and drug possession, and 1st District Judge Spencer D. Walsh suspended his prison terms in favor of three years of probation with treatment, counseling and a parenting class. item.title: Trump breaks silence on nationwide ground stop and demands more money from Congress
item.description:
After staying quiet since Friday's nationwide ground stop stranded travelers, President Donald Trump on Sunday used it to press Congress for more air traffic control money, posting that the upgrade shouldn't come in "drips and drabs" and blaming the Biden administration for leaving the system worse. Congress already gave the FAA $12.5 billion in last year's tax package, which Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has called a down payment, and Duffy has said the trouble started when contractor L3Harris swapped old copper wire for fiber; after that work at an El Dorado, Ark., site, a problem cascaded from an Amarillo, Texas, facility. L3Harris is now running diagnostics on routers from both sites, Duffy said, adding on CBS that despite lingering delays he expected flights at full capacity by late Sunday into Monday.

John Curtis is undecided on advancing Cissie Graham Lynch, Billy Graham's granddaughter and President Donald Trump's pick for ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom, over a podcast episode in which she drew lines between Christianity and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. item.title: Wasatch County ordered to pay $400K in Daniels Canyon Mine dispute
item.description:
4th District Judge Jennifer Mabey on Nov. 6 ordered Wasatch County to pay Maverick Rock $404,151.50 in attorney fees, cutting $75,000 for duplicative work from the roughly $479,000 the company sought, after ruling in April that the county had failed its legal duty to hold a public hearing on the company's plan to expand mining into a 426-acre site in Daniels Canyon. The fees aren't due until the case is finally resolved, with both the damages claim and the county's appeal still pending; Councilman Erik Rowland said the council was "unanimous in our disagreement with this mine."

item.title: Red Cross honors Utah volunteers for service during disasters and emergencies
item.description:
Volunteers make up about 90% of the Red Cross workforce, the organization said, and on Saturday the American Red Cross of Utah honored about 35 of them at the Utah Capitol for their work after wildfires, floods and other emergencies. Jeremiah LaFranca, executive director of the Greater Salt Lake Chapter, called this year incredibly difficult, saying summer wildfires kept volunteers working "on a constant basis for several months in a row." Two volunteers received the Clara Barton Honor Award for Meritorious Volunteer Leadership, among them Kathy Allen of the Northern Utah and Southwest Wyoming Chapter, recognized for 47 years with the Red Cross.

item.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump on Washington public golf course redevelopment
item.description:
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes on Saturday issued a temporary restraining order barring the government, through Nov. 28 or a further order, from closing East Potomac Park and its public golf course during their usual hours, a day before the course was to shut for 15 months so President Donald Trump could rebuild it as a championship-level venue. Trump's own October social media posts announcing the closure weighed heavily in the ruling, with Reyes writing that they indicate the plan is final and that the Park Service will close the park, and "Both points favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order." The Justice Department said the order does not stop planning for a new course, while Democracy Forward, which represents the DC Preservation League and two local golfers who sued in February, praised it.

item.title: Roy homeowner frustrated after car crashes through his fence for second time in 14 months
item.description:
For the second time in under 14 months, a vehicle tore through David Osborne's front fence near 4800 South and 2950 West in Roy, this time overnight into Saturday while he and his wife slept in their basement after driving home from Las Vegas, leaving tire marks, debris and fence pieces across the yard. Osborne believes drivers speeding near a roundabout are making the road dangerous, says he has asked police for more speed enforcement and wants speed bumps or similar changes considered, and plans to take the issue to the police chief or city council next. A woman was hit and taken to a hospital in the earlier crash, in September 2025, and Osborne said he put up a shed partly because that vehicle nearly reached the house; Roy police had not told KSL whether anyone was hurt this time.

item.title: Police lift evacuation after bomb found near ethanol plant in central Illinois
item.description:
Authorities in Peoria lifted a 1-mile evacuation order Saturday that had pushed hundreds of residents from their homes after a bomb was found Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables ethanol plant, with police saying state, federal and local searchers had "found no other items of concern". The device had already been rendered safe, no injuries or arrests have been reported, and FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley said the bureau is investigating but declined to give details. Mayor Rita Ali had told WMBD-TV that the plant stores ethanol and other volatile chemicals, "and so that's what alarms us."

item.title: Holiday meals donated to 100 Utah military families
item.description:
Food insecurity is "really big in our military right now," said Bridgette Sanchez, a program manager with Operation Homefront, who said about 28% of military families report being unsure where their next meal will come from. On Saturday in Centerville, the nonprofit gave holiday meals to 100 military families who had asked for help, at an event backed by Swire Coca-Cola, Walmart and other sponsors. Roughly 60 more Utah families are on the group's waiting list, and Sanchez said Operation Homefront is working on a second event to reach them as the holidays approach.

item.title: SpaceX's Starship returns from orbit, captured by launch pad arms in a dramatic first
item.description:
SpaceX caught its Starship upper stage in the launch tower's mechanical arms Saturday, the first time a Starship coming back from space has been captured, after a 22-hour flight in which it circled Earth 14 times and released 26 Starlink satellites. The company missed the double catch it wanted after the first-stage booster's guidance system, sensing it was out of position, triggered its self-destruction, a failure engineers are still investigating, and SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines had quit too soon on the way down. SpaceX said the catch shows Starship can be fully reused, and NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, whose agency is paying billions for Starship to carry Artemis crews to the lunar surface, wrote on X that it was "almost magic".

item.title: Johannes Gutenberg — the long-presumed Father of Printing — is having his 'paternity' challenged
item.description:
The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type is Korea's Jikji Simche Yojeol, a Buddhist text produced decades before Johannes Gutenberg's 42-line Bible, and a new 672-page volume, From Jikji to Gutenberg, co-edited by University of Utah Marriott Library preservation head Randy Silverman and Cathleen Baker, gathers essays from scholars worldwide on how the technology developed. Silverman, who spent about 25 years as a preservationist before learning of Jikji while visiting Cheongju, where it was printed, on a trip to Korea at UNESCO's invitation, calls the book "a long-overdue step toward setting the record straight" and argues the West owes much to Asian ingenuity. Although UNESCO placed Jikji on its Memory of the World register alongside Gutenberg's Bible in 2001, most Westerners likely still know little of it, a gap the project also aims to close with an online exhibition and a children's picture book.

item.title: Salt Lake City International Airport activated pre-prepared emergency plans to handle ground stop
item.description:
Salt Lake City International Airport expects flight operations to be fully back to normal by Sunday evening after Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop led to 138 cancellations there, airport officials said. Communications director Nancy Volmer said staff immediately activated emergency plans prepared in advance, protocols usually set off by bad weather, and that some planes already on the tarmac had to return to the gate and unload, though no diverted flights ended up landing in Salt Lake City. About 216 flights had departed since midnight Saturday, and by 5 p.m. help-desk and baggage lines had shrunk, with the operations team telling Volmer things were "actually running very smoothly."

item.title: How P.F. Chang's new CEO is bringing 'theatrics' back to its dining rooms
item.description:
P.F. Chang's CEO Jim Mazany, the chain's fourth leader in roughly two years, has tried to pull takeout-heavy customers back into dining rooms with tableside spectacle like a $49 sushi boat wreathed in dry-ice fog, a dish that has generated $2 million in sales since June. Along with a return to scratch cooking and a "barbell" menu that pairs $13.99 deals with pricier dishes, the changes lifted traffic more than 5% from a year earlier and pushed third-quarter same-restaurant sales up nearly 10%, the chain's first sales growth since 2023. Mazany, who said the chain had been "competing with people's couches," said the momentum has sped up plans to possibly go public next year, and the company plans 40 more U.S. locations over five years.

item.title: Utah governor recognized by Time 100 on climate
item.description:
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox was named to Time's 2026 list of 100 climate leaders as one of its few conservatives, a nod to his growing reputation as a Republican champion of small modular reactors, geothermal power and faster permitting through his Operation Gigawatt push. Cox said Utah "continues to show that we don't have to choose between protecting the environment and building prosperity," while Danielle Franz of the Republican-oriented American Conservation Coalition praised his leadership. Not everyone agreed: Scott Braden of the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance called the pick "baffling," citing Cox's support for shrinking national monuments in southern Utah and a state focus on nuclear over wind, solar and battery storage.

item.title: Pope laments violence enveloping Peru as he ministers in his former diocese
item.description:
Back in Chiclayo, where he was bishop from 2014 to 2023, Pope Leo XIV prayed Saturday at the cathedral about the darkness of rising crime in Peru, whose homicide rate has nearly doubled in five years, then flew by helicopter to the remote mountain town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, a trip he once made himself by pickup truck. There, Leo said selfishness, injustice and evil are "not overcome by brutality, but by prayer, patience and perseverance in denouncing what is wrong". Indigenous representatives from the San Juan Bautista de Catacaos community, who say companies tied to the Sodalitium Christianae Vitae, suppressed by Pope Francis last year, tried to force them off ancestral land, used the visit to press the church for justice and reparations.

item.title: Romney has a 2028 prediction — but there's a catch
item.description:
In a statement to the Deseret News, former Sen. Mitt Romney said Vice President JD Vance is still the likeliest 2028 Republican nominee, a call he first made in late 2024, though he conceded it is less certain after the GOP's midterm losses and that "predictions like this can change pretty dramatically with events." Romney said Vance's prospects may depend more on how President Donald Trump performs in his final two years than on "anything he might do" himself. Vance, the hopeful most closely tied to Trump, blamed the party's losses on the Iran war and the gas prices it drove up, a statement that appeared to break with the president even though both men insisted it wasn't.

item.title: Man sentenced to probation for gun possession after second trial leads to acquittal for killing
item.description:
Patrick Koaneil Brown, 48, charged in the fatal shooting of Darnell Brown (no relation) after an April 2021 road rage confrontation in Murray, was acquitted of manslaughter by a second jury in September, after an appeals court reversed his 2022 manslaughter conviction, and 3rd District Judge Adam Mow sentenced him Nov. 5 to 36 months of probation on a restricted-person weapons count. Mow suspended the one-to-15-year prison term, credited Brown with 1,979 days already served and ordered cognitive behavioral and anger management courses, telling Brown, who questioned the need after the acquittal, that the conviction was "based on you choosing to show a firearm at a time when I don't think there was a threat posed." The weapons charge, which Brown asked the judge rather than the jury to decide, rested on earlier Alabama convictions for bank robbery and aggravated assault.

item.title: US air travel schedule should recover from ground stop by the end of Sunday, FAA says
item.description:
Airlines canceled thousands of U.S. flights Saturday after Friday's ground stop of more than four hours, the longest nationwide halt in 25 years, and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said schedules should return to normal by the end of Sunday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a contractor swapping old copper wire for fiber somehow overloaded the system, that officials were investigating whether contractor "incompetence" or a faulty wire was to blame, and that "you will have more of these" as he faulted Congress for not approving more money for new technology. In Utah, 65 flights left Salt Lake City International after the stop lifted at 6:28 p.m. Friday, according to airport spokesperson Nancy Volmer, while the Utes' and BYU's Saturday games and Weber State's game were all pushed back.

item.title: New Orleans port sues to get control of tanker that crashed into cruise ship on Mississippi River
item.description:
Hours after the 520-foot tanker Atlantic Asphalt apparently lost steering and rammed the docked American Heritage river cruise boat in New Orleans on Friday, the port's board of commissioners sued over at least $1 million in terminal damage, and a judge issued a warrant giving federal officials control of the tanker, whose owner is a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation. All 197 people aboard the cruise boat survived even though it rolled onto its side and dumped passenger Joe Knab and roughly 100 others into the Mississippi; 32 people went to the hospital, none in critical condition, and eight were still there Saturday. Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll pointed to the life vests passengers had put on before the roll as likely the biggest factor in everyone surviving, and Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said moving the cruise boat could take weeks.

item.description:
Randy Alan Toney, 43, convicted by a jury in September on eight counts of arson endangering human life for grass fires set beside I-70 near the Utah-Colorado line this summer, received three years of probation from 7th District Judge Don Torgerson, who suspended the prison terms and ordered no restitution. Toney left jail Oct. 21 after roughly four months and must stay away from alcohol and drugs while on probation. According to the charges, nine fires were set in all, with no reported injuries or structure damage, and a trooper responding to a 911 report spotted a man running along the freeway shoulder, with Toney's pants "actively smoking."

item.title: New 'The Cat in the Hat' is fun whimsical chaos that will win over audiences
item.description:
Valerie Cameron's review says the new animated The Cat in the Hat, directed by Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja with Bill Hader voicing the Cat, is that rare animated film both adults and kids will enjoy, pairing a well-written adaptation with silliness and vibrant animation. The film adds a Seussian world beyond the wall, which Cameron likens to Monsters, Inc., where creatures work to lift children's spirits, and it hands the mischief-prone Cat one final, big assignment: cheering up Gabby, a miserable tween who has just moved to a new town, and her brother Sebastian. Cameron writes that adults and children at her screening laughed together for nearly the whole 1-hour-47-minute PG film, recommends seeing it in a theater and calls it "a winner."

item.title: Salt Lake City's historic Pioneer Park gets a makeover. Can it change perceptions?
item.description:
Salt Lake City reopened Pioneer Park after an $18 million renovation that Mayor Erin Mendenhall said finished under budget and early, adding two dog parks, an events pavilion and promenade, an all-abilities playground with mist features and more than 120 trees. Because residents have long complained of camping, needles and crime near the area's historic homeless services, the city built a park ranger station and plans nightly bathroom lockups and regular police foot and bike patrols, and Tyler Murdock, deputy director of the city's public lands department, acknowledged "It's no secret we've had challenges." Downtown resident Sam Morse called the project a nice facelift that won't fix the area's long-term problems, while Police Chief Brian Redd is hopeful that drawing more people to the park will discourage illegal activity.

item.title: Labor organizer defeats longtime Utah Republican lawmaker
item.description:
Democrat Blake Townsend, a 32-year-old labor organizer making his first run for office, unseated Taylorsville Republican Rep. Jim Dunnigan, first elected to the House in 2002, winning House District 36 with 53.3% of the vote as Democrats were on track to flip 14 GOP-held House seats and end the Republican supermajority. Dunnigan, 73, blamed widespread dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump — "I think it was a national tsunami" — and warned that the loss of so many veteran lawmakers means a big learning curve, while Townsend said the voters he met worried about affordability and wanted a new generation. University of Utah political scientist Tim Chambless called the Democratic gains "very huge" because Republicans no longer hold a veto-proof House majority.

Ogden Valley, the Weber County city incorporated last January, has dropped its bid for a 512.6% property tax increase, the largest percentage hike proposed in Utah this year, and will run on a budget of about $5.9 million rather than $7.4 million, most notably by trimming road improvements. The Utah State Tax Commission blocked the hike over a deadline missed during incorporation, and the city's pro bono lawyers have asked the Utah Supreme Court to rule anyway because the dispute "extends well beyond Ogden Valley City" as other new cities form. Council member Kay Hoogland called it "a one-year problem," with a transportation utility fee and a 6% municipal energy tax covering part of the gap and a tax increase possible for 2027-2028.

item.title: The US flu season is off to a very early start. It's targeting the South and West now
item.description:
Seven states, among them California, Texas, Washington and Louisiana, were at high flu activity levels last week, compared with just two a week earlier, according to the CDC, which estimates at least 2.6 million illnesses and 2,100 deaths so far in an unusually early season that is hitting Louisiana hardest. Most cases trace to an H1N1 strain whose mutations could help it slip past immune defenses, though Johns Hopkins immunologist Andrew Pekosz said early data suggest the vaccine "can recognize" the virus. With doctors expecting Thanksgiving travel to speed the spread, LSU infectious diseases specialist Fred Lopez urged anyone still unvaccinated to get a shot now, even if they already had the flu this fall.

item.description:
UtahRadon.org's 2026 State of Radon in Utah report, drawn from more than 18,000 home tests between September 2025 and September 2026, found 69.6% of homes above 2.0 pCi/L, the point at which the EPA recommends considering action, with elevated readings in every region regardless of income or home age. Lehi lung cancer patient Kerri Robbins, whose home measured 31.3 pCi/L, urged continuous monitors, and Utah Radon Services' TJ Mellars said a mitigation system runs around $2,000, though no Utah law requires testing. Grantsville, Perry, Smithfield and Providence had the highest shares of homes above the WHO's 2.7 pCi/L reference level, around 80%, while Washington County came in at 20%.

Kirt Michaelis, who has spent the last 18 years as vice president and chief financial officer of Mountainland Technical College, was unanimously chosen Friday by the state's higher education board to become the school's next president, starting Dec. 1. Board member Jeremy Hafen called Michaelis "part of the heart and soul" of the college, and a USHE release credits Michaelis with helping ensure 99% of graduating cohorts finished debt-free. item.title: The US and Mexico are on the verge of forfeiting a major health victory. Here's what to know
item.description:
A Pan American Health Organization advisory commission is reviewing genetic evidence this week to decide whether measles has spread continuously for a year or more in the U.S. and Mexico, and experts expect both countries to lose the elimination status the U.S. has held since 2000 and Mexico since 2016; Cleveland health director Dr. David Margolius said the decision represents "us moving backward". The U.S. has logged more than 5,400 confirmed cases and eight measles-associated deaths this year, its worst year for the illness since 1991, while Mexico has reported more than 20,500 cases and 50 deaths since its surge began early last year. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said losing the designation won't change the federal approach, but many public health experts fault what they describe as a muted federal response and blame Health Secretary Robert F. Investigators believe she was napping without having shifted the Chevrolet 1500 into park and probably pressed the gas in her sleep; when detectives left a similar Chevy 1500 in drive in the same stall, it stayed put until the accelerator was pressed. A senior official said the session should open nuclear arms talks, which Trump wants to include China after New START expired in February, but no agreements are expected, and Beijing, with more than 600 warheads by Pentagon estimates against over 5,000 each for the U.S. and Russia, has shown little appetite for a pact. Webb has had multiple surgeries for injuries including a shattered vertebra and two broken ankles, some of which could take up to a year to heal, said Bailey, adding that the family hopes for the community's prayers. item.title: Utah woman hopes DNA testing will finally bring home relative killed in World War II
item.description:
Courtney Draper, a Salt Lake City lawyer captured by Japanese forces in 1942 who survived the little-known Mindanao Death March and years in prison camps, was killed in January 1945 when American planes bombed the Enoura Maru at Takao Harbor, and his remains have never been identified. Noel, whose grandfather was Draper's cousin and who also attended George Washington University, hopes a Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency project that exhumed 430 unidentified remains in Hawaii and the Philippines in 2022 and 2023 for forensic and DNA analysis will finally bring him home. Dickson, who credits much of her success to longtime co-host Grant Nielsen, plans to teach full time and spend more time with family, saying she "can't fathom" no longer setting an alarm for 2:15.

item.title: Family Dollar to pay $63M settlement after Utah, FTC allege company overcharged customers
item.description:
Family Dollar, which runs more than 7,000 stores including 55 in Utah, will pay $63 million to settle a complaint from the FTC, Utah and 16 other states alleging its registers charged more than shelf tags, ads, mailers, its website and its app showed. The complaint says the chain has collected millions in overcharges since 2023 despite thousands of failed inspections, and that many stores sit in what the company itself calls "food deserts," where it may be one of the only places to buy food. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown said the settlement "puts money back in consumers' pockets"; a similar suit Utah, the FTC and other states filed against Dollar General in October is ongoing.

item.title: Microsoft outage shows the risks of relying on a single technology provider for essential services
item.description:
Microsoft 365 services including Outlook, Teams and Copilot stayed disrupted into a second day Friday after Downdetector received reports from 74 countries and territories in the first hour, with Microsoft tracing the problem to a technical issue during an upgrade that followed "a recent network change" and saying there was no sign of malicious activity. The fallout ranged from a Manchester judge sending jurors home and British police losing online crime reporting to pharmacy prescription delays and email trouble for ministries in Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway. The outage renewed some European calls for "digital sovereignty", and British lawmaker Chi Onwurah said it shows again how Britain's digital infrastructure lacks resilience and depends on a handful of U.S. providers.

item.title: Wrangle weeds, win cash: Hurricane mayor hosts 'Tumbleweed Takeover'
item.description:
Hurricane Mayor Clark Fawcett, who says residents have sent photos of tumbleweeds blocking front doors and garages, is hosting a "Tumbleweed Takeover" on Saturday morning, a two-hour cleanup on state land at 1375 W. State Street for which volunteers should bring gloves and shovels. Fawcett has pledged to pull at least 1,000 of the invasive plants personally, has cleared 500 so far, and is offering $250, $200 and $150 to residents who clear the most, entered by submitting before-and-after photos. The event is the latest of the mayor's "Mayor Meetups," and Fawcett said that, if nothing else, the goal is to raise awareness.

item.title: Petition argues against potential early closure of Utah County school
item.description:
Nebo School District's board is expected to vote Dec. 9 on whether to close Payson's Wilson Elementary in May 2027, years ahead of the 2033 date set when the city agreed in 2023 to buy the building, which Payson now wants to own by summer 2027. A petition started by Rachel Hansen, with 500 signatures as of Friday, says the district is "rushing this closure to 2027" and warns of lost Title I funds and poor outreach to families who don't speak English, while the district points to declining enrollment and says consolidation would lift building use from about 63% to about 79%. Nadine Kay, who taught first grade there for 16 years, called the school "the heartbeat of the neighborhood."

item.title: Burglar caused $70K in damage to warehouse looking for copper wires, police say
item.description:
West Valley City police say a man seen on surveillance video breaking into a vacant warehouse on Decker Lake Boulevard that the state recently bought cut copper wiring with an angle grinder, ripped into walls and ceiling panels, and broke "every breaker box" in the building, causing over $70,000 in damage. When officers arrived Thursday morning, Casey Steven Kalipetsis, 48, sped off in an F-150, drove into oncoming traffic and ended up hitting a cinderblock wall, then said he had taken too much bath salts, according to the affidavit. Police say Kalipetsis has numerous theft and burglary convictions, and he was booked into jail on burglary, DUI and other investigative counts.

item.title: Community rallies around family of 22-year-old killed in crash involving Box Elder County sheriff
item.description:
Family friend Chelsea Frei is trying to raise $7,000 through a GoFundMe to send the family of Katie Sue Ruth Huggins, 22, to Disneyland, a place Katie loved, after she died from injuries in an Oct. 27 motorcycle crash, still under investigation, that involved Box Elder County Sheriff Kevin Potter. Katie, nicknamed "Goofy Sue," was one of four daughters adopted by single mother Amie Huggins, and relatives said she became an organ donor. In a statement Thursday, Amie Huggins said that on the family's final Disney trip, Katie had told them she felt, for the first time, that she belonged with everyone.

item.title: Advisory issued as rain, snow return to Utah after recent lull
item.description:
A fast-moving storm sliding in from Nevada is expected to bring valley rain and mountain snow to Utah Friday night into Saturday, with a winter weather advisory for the southern mountains calling for 5-10 inches above 9,000 feet, and 2-8 inches possible in other ranges, more in the Cottonwood Canyons. It should clear the Wasatch Front's inversion haze and drop highs from the low 60s into the upper 40s or low 50s, and it is the first of three storms expected over the next week, with the third possibly bringing snow or a rain-snow mix to the valleys. Some long-range models suggest the mountains could pile up multiple feet of snow across the cycle, a potential boost for ski resorts waiting to open.

item.title: Pineview Reservoir pipeline project advancing; fish population managing
item.description:
Ogden's new pipeline section across the largely drained bed of Pineview Reservoir, one piece of a $100 million project replacing 6.4 miles of aging line, could be finished in December, slightly ahead of the original early-January target, with Ogden's Justin Anderson saying the work is "going really well" and back on track. While the bed is exposed, the Division of Wildlife Resources plans to place around 1,300 fish structures, likely in January with volunteer help, funded by $200,000 from Ogden and $50,000 from the state Department of Natural Resources. DWR aquatics program manager Chris Penne said the fish pushed toward the dam end are "doing fine" and that, based on historical data, many species are expected to recover within about five years of refilling.

item.title: SpaceX is set to make an audacious grab for 'holy grail' of rocketry. Here are the risks
item.description:
SpaceX was set Friday to try, for the first time, to recover every piece of Starship, including landing the 171-foot upper spacecraft upright in the grip of its South Texas launch tower after a trip to orbit, a step toward the fully reusable system the company calls the "holy grail" of rocketry. CNN's Jackie Wattles lays out the risks, from Raptor engines that have quit mid-flight, as one did on September's Flight 14 before Musk prompted controllers to reconsider skipping the push to orbit, to a reentry path that crosses land over northern Mexico and southern Texas. Joseph Gonzalez, who teaches aerospace engineering at the University of Illinois, said strong results could put SpaceX on track for "a fully reusable rocket in the next two or three years."

item.title: Microsoft outage means no email chimes or message pings, but still we stayed online
item.description:
An AP look at the global Microsoft 365 outage, which stretched into Friday the 13th and could reach as many as 450 million paid users, finds that people mostly stayed glued to their screens instead of going offline. Brands piled on with jokes — Burger King told whoever was fixing the outage to "take your time" and get a Whopper — while workers moved meetings to WhatsApp or turned to Xbox. One Redditor said the quiet office felt like a social event and asked, "Is this what the 90s felt like?"

item.description:
Microsoft Outlook went dark for nearly 17 hours starting Thursday morning, cutting email and chat for hundreds of thousands of users including in Utah after several servers became "unexpectedly unavailable." Down Detector logged more than 131,000 reports by 11:14 a.m., and Microsoft began returning servers to service that afternoon while shifting traffic to alternate routes. Early Friday the company reported "improvements in key scenarios" but warned intermittent outages could still occur.

item.title: Peru's Chiclayo welcomes its former shepherd home, and revels in pope's love
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV returned Friday to Chiclayo, the northern Peruvian diocese he led as bishop from 2014 until 2023, where organizers expected as many as a million people at his first big Mass in the country. Residents recalled his closeness to the poor through COVID-19, floods and a surge of Venezuelan migrants, and local shops sell "Papaletas" bearing his image. "Even though he's now Pope Leo XIV, he hasn't forgotten about his homeland," said poster vendor Rolando Antonio Mendoza.

item.title: US military downs 2 Iranian attack drones as Iran claims a strike on a US radar in Bahrain
item.description:
The U.S. military said Friday it shot down two Iranian attack drones headed toward Bahrain with no injuries or damage, rejecting a Revolutionary Guard claim that it had struck a U.S. early-warning radar there after a U.S. strike on a telecommunications pole in the Iranian port of Sirik. The Guard also said a liquefied petroleum gas tanker hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings, and neither claim could be independently verified. In Tehran, thousands joined funerals for the remains of 110 soldiers from the Iran-Iraq war, with services for 240 more held in other cities.

item.title: 'Our mission is to empower our youth': Latinos in Action to mark 25 years of operation
item.description:
Latinos in Action, the Orem-based program José Enriquez started as a Timpview High School class in 2000, is holding a 25th Anniversary Gala in Salt Lake City on Friday that is expected to draw about 400 students. It now offers more than 300 elective classes at over 250 schools, mostly in Utah and Florida, built around leadership, tutoring younger kids, service, college readiness and financial literacy. Enriquez, an immigrant from El Salvador, said he wanted to "create our own Latino heroes within our own system."

Microsoft slipped 1.4% in premarket trading as its global outage continued, while investors awaited October producer price data after September's report showed the biggest increase since December 2022. Brent crude rose to $96.04 a barrel after President Donald Trump said the U.S. didn't "need a deal with Iran."

item.title: Why this Utah resort could be the state's biggest winner this winter
item.description:
Meteorologist Jennifer Broome named Brian Head one of the "snowiest adventure towns" for this winter in Outside Magazine, writing that it "is in a sweet spot for Super El Niño's elevated snow amounts." The Climate Prediction Center gives most of Utah equal chances for precipitation through February, but southern Utah has slightly better odds of above-average moisture, and its January–March outlook tilts wetter statewide. The forecast follows one of Utah's worst snow seasons on record, which produced the lowest snowpack since records began in 1930.

The light saber Darth Vader used in the Cloud City duel of "The Empire Strikes Back," and also in "Return of the Jedi," sold for $4.875 million Thursday at Heritage Auctions' Ultimate Star Wars Auction in Dallas. Heritage says it is a world auction record for any "Star Wars" collectible, topping the $3.75 million it got in July for Luke Skywalker's light saber and severed-hand effects rig. The sale also offered 27 other light sabers and material from Episodes I through IX.

item.title: Provo GOP lawmaker holds narrow lead in tight Utah House race
item.description:
Rep. Lisa Shepherd, R-Provo, led Democrat Alan Jimenez by 228 votes in House District 61 as of late Thursday, with a winner due early next week once Utah County reports its last few thousand ballots. Shepherd blamed the tight race on a hard national climate for Republicans and backlash over the failed Amendment B, while Jimenez, a cybersecurity worker running for the first time, said voters feel ignored and see the Legislature as lacking transparency. The contest follows Democrat David Chappell's defeat of longtime Rep. Norm Thurston in House District 62, a breakthrough in a county with no Democratic legislator in several decades, amid statewide losses that cost House Republicans their supermajority for the first time in decades.

item.title: Protecting babies from RSV during the holiday season
item.description:
With holiday gatherings approaching, Carolyn Reynolds of Intermountain Children's Health says RSV cases in Utah are low for now but expects them to rise between Thanksgiving and Christmas, a concern because infants' immature immune systems struggle to fight off viruses and RSV is the leading cause of infant hospitalization nationwide. Protection is available through a maternal vaccine given at 32 to 36 weeks of pregnancy or an antibody shot for eligible newborns, and the 16,000 Utah babies protected in the 2024-2025 season were nine times less likely to be hospitalized. Reynolds urges parents not to pass babies around to people who may be sick, and most insurance covers the RSV shot, with free doses for uninsured families through Utah's Vaccines for Children program.

item.title: Intoxicated driver hit car with 7 juveniles inside, police say
item.description:
Six of seven juveniles riding in a Chevy Malibu were taken by ambulance to St. George Regional Hospital after the car was hit in Hurricane around 1:40 a.m. Oct. 24 by a Honda Civic that dispatchers said ran a red light at high speed; one suffered a ruptured spleen and five spinal fractures, and another a dislocated hip, according to a police booking affidavit. The Civic's driver, Victor Manuel Lomei, 21, of LaVerkin, was charged Thursday with DUI, reckless driving and several counts of negligently causing injury after police reported "an odor of an alcoholic beverage" and found an empty beer bottle. The affidavit says Lomei later claimed he believed he had fallen asleep at the wheel.

item.title: Firefighters with cancer have workers' compensation claims denied, despite Utah law
item.description:
West Jordan firefighter and paramedic Justin Young waited 111 days for Travelers Insurance to rule on his workers' compensation claim for recurring prostate cancer, only to be denied because the cancer was first found before Utah's expanded firefighter-cancer presumption took effect. Rep. Casey Snider, who sponsored that expansion, called the outcome "ludicrous" and said he has heard of 30 to 40 firefighters caught in the same gap, which he and Rep. Jordan Teuscher said lawmakers plan to fix next session. A new Firefighter Cancer Benefit Trust Fund meant to help during such delays has not paid out yet, and Young has begun treatment on his own health insurance.

item.title: Republicans score rare blue-to-red flip in Maine during midterm landslide
item.description:
Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage narrowly defeated Democratic state auditor Matt Dunlap for the open 2nd Congressional District seat, the only blue-to-red flip of the midterms not driven by redistricting; the AP's call came Thursday, once ranked choice tabulation finished. The rural, more conservative district, which Trump carried by 9 points two years ago, had been held by retiring moderate Democrat Jared Golden, while Democrats have flipped 44 seats nationally. LePage, who once described himself as "Donald Trump before Donald Trump became popular" but has also criticized Trump's tariffs on Canada, vowed to oppose whatever is "bad for Maine" once in Washington.

item.title: Arrest made in fatal Salt Lake City shooting
item.description:
Salt Lake City police arrested Ernesto Rosendo Flores, 24, originally from Las Vegas, on suspicion of murder and obstruction of justice in the Nov. 7 killing of Evan Cole, 32, who a witness said was shot near 475 W. 600 South after getting out of his truck and walking up to the driver's door of a white car that had pulled in behind him. Detectives tied Flores to the car through surveillance video and body camera footage from an earlier traffic stop, and cellphone data placed Flores in the area, the affidavit says. The white Audi A5 with Nevada "Raiders" plates and the suspected murder weapon have not been recovered, and police are seeking witnesses who saw it and a gray pickup heading north on I-15 that morning.

item.title: California man accused of human smuggling in southern Utah
item.description:
After his arrest in southern Utah, Hector Pec Tecum, 50, of Los Angeles, admitted charging passengers $300 each for a Nov. 10 drive from California to Denver, keeping what was left after fuel as profit, according to a police booking affidavit. Asked whether his riders were in the U.S. illegally, he said one had a visa but added, "I wouldn't be transporting them if they weren't illegal". The case, which brought three second-degree felony human smuggling charges in 5th District Court, followed a tip to a Washington County detective on a Homeland Security task force, and one person from an earlier immigration arrest told investigators he paid Pec Tecum $500 for a ride to Florida.

item.title: Colorado mom: Son's online game leads to missing Utah teen
item.description:
Colorado mom Khristina Tresp told KSL that her teenage son met a girl while playing Among Us shortly before Halloween and, after the chat moved to Discord, learned she was a runaway being held and hurt by an older man. Using a name the 17-year-old from Garden City supplied, Tresp searched county property records and sent her Zillow photos until she recognized the house, a turning point for a Utah teen who had been gone almost a year and a half. Adam Hunter Harmel now faces a federal charge of transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity, and court documents say Harmel may have enticed other minors and attempted to abduct at least one, leading law enforcement to seek information from victims nationwide.

item.title: 1,000 Thanksgiving meals for veterans in SLC, Ogden by Ken Garff employees
item.description:
Ken Garff employees are assembling 1,000 Thanksgiving bags, each with a frozen turkey, sides and a pumpkin pie, for veterans and active-duty service members, to be handed out first-come, first-served at drive-through events Friday morning at Salt Lake City's VA hospital and Ogden's VA clinic. Community and events coordinator Kate Terry said veterans now call ahead to ask whether the event is happening again, and that amid rising living costs "there's a huge need, and we're just trying to make a small dent in that" for people who sacrificed for the country. Those picking up a meal must show a military ID, a VA medical card or a Veterans Identification Card.

item.title: BLM rounds up hundreds of wild horses near Dugway
item.description:
The Bureau of Land Management is using a helicopter to drive wild horses into corrals this week near Dugway in the Cedar Mountain Herd Management Area, aiming to remove about 500 from a herd it estimates at roughly 660, well above the 200 to 400 the agency believes the land can sustain. Chad Hunter, head of the BLM's Utah wild horse and burro program, said he thinks it has been about four years since the last roundup there and that numbers double "about every 4 to 5 years"; removed horses go to corrals near Delta and Axtell for veterinary checks ahead of adoption or other placement. Jan Drake, who heads Wild Horses of the West and works with the BLM to dart mares with birth control, wants the horses kept on the range "in numbers that they can be healthy", though some advocacy groups consider roundups and sterilization cruel and have sued in the past to stop them.

item.title: Man charged in connection with 12 hour standoff in Yalecrest neighborhood
item.description:
Elliott Jones, 52, was charged Thursday with five second-degree felony counts of assaulting an officer and causing property damage over a Nov. 6 confrontation at his Yalecrest home that began after he called police about an eviction notice. Charges say Jones asked an officer whether he wanted a gunfight and pointed a hand shaped like a gun before four gunshots were heard after he went back inside, and that after a loudspeaker call-out he came out and threw an axe that hit the windshield of an armored Bearcat, causing about $10,000 in damage. Tear gas failed to end the roughly 12-hour standoff, and Unified police SWAT members eventually entered and arrested Jones Saturday morning, finding more than a half-dozen guns inside.

item.title: 'You can't land where we're at': Report sheds light on fire that killed 4 firefighters
item.description:
A 95-page federal investigation released Thursday into the June fire west of Grand Junction that killed firefighters Emily Barker, Nick Hutcherson, Sydney Watson and Nathan Matthews found that extreme weather and very low fuel moisture drove the blaze, while aging radios, network saturation, dispatch vacancies and trainees, and overlapping helicopter frequencies hampered coordination. The U.S. Wildland Fire Service and U.S. Forest Service concluded that the tragedy reflected "the cumulative effects of known limitations operating under extraordinary tempo and conditions". The report recounts Barker telling a helicopter not to land at the crew's site and, according to the surviving firefighter, offering her own shelter when the survivor struggled to close theirs.

Ten faiths that took part last year are opening their doors for the third Cache Valley Tour of Faiths, a two-week event sponsored by Cache Community Connections that begins Friday, with each congregation offering a 15-minute introduction followed by questions from visitors. item.description:
Tracie Palmer, a senior account executive who spent 14 years at KSL, died Oct. 19 after a nearly two-year fight with breast cancer, having kept working for 22 months after her diagnosis. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani shaved off the trimmed beard that had become part of his signature look and debuted a standalone mustache while handing out water at the New York City Marathon, prompting The Cut to dub him "Mayor Mustache" and setting off online debate. CNN notes that mustaches remain rare among American politicians, with John Bolton long the best-known example in Washington. Derek Thomas Horne, 43, previously convicted in 2009 and, in federal court, in 2018 for online offenses involving minors, was arrested Oct. 11 by Weber County deputies and charged with first-degree felony enticing a minor plus a sex offender registry violation. Prosecutors say Horne contacted an undercover Facebook profile posing as a 14-year-old girl and that his messages grew "increasingly explicit" despite repeated reminders of her age, and charges say he admitted using social media while knowing his federal probation barred it. Probation reports describe earlier lapses, including having his smartphone taken away in 2024 and "risky online behavior" on a monitored phone issued in 2025; Horne pleaded not guilty Oct. 20.

Texts cited in new charges show former BYU wide receiver Parker Kingston, 22, telling a friend he "cracked her," which he later told investigators meant having sex, and the woman alleges she told him "no" four times before he had intercourse with her without consent in St. George. Kingston contends she never refused, though he says that an hour after leaving he got a text from her claiming she had refused. Washington County prosecutors refiled the first-degree felony rape charge Thursday, after 5th District Judge Jay Winward refused to delay a July trial and dismissed the case when prosecutors said the woman was not ready to testify.

Nolin Jeffery Maurer, 64, who had been head custodian at Eden's Snowcrest Junior High, was sentenced Monday to consecutive terms adding up to at least six years and as much as life after pleading guilty in September to rape, forcible sexual abuse and distribution of material harmful to a minor. A plea deal dropped four other counts, including object rape and forcible sodomy, and original charging documents place the abuse at a Pleasant View home and van, not on school property. The case began when the girl's father found journal entries and an unauthorized phone, and a forensic review of that phone turned up Snapchat and text exchanges that included requests for explicit images, according to the plea deal.

item.title: Officers, injured victims testify as man is ordered to stand trial for 4 deaths at WestFest
item.description:
A 3rd District judge ordered Matthiaz Centre Lauti Ioane-Register, now 18, to face trial on four aggravated murder counts and multiple felony firearm-discharge charges in the June 15, 2025, WestFest shooting at Centennial Park that killed an 8-month-old boy, a 41-year-old woman eight weeks pregnant and Hassan Lugundi, 18, whom a detective described as the intended target. West Valley City officer David Hagues testified that he ran toward the then-16-year-old as he kept firing, and two teens shot in the arm said they still occasionally feel pain after months of recovery. Another officer testified that while in custody at the scene, Ioane-Register said he "knew what he was shooting at" and "didn't shoot a baby."

item.title: Salt Lake man accused of killing roommate admits shooting was 'impulsive'
item.description:
Charging documents say James Stacey Riedman, 47, eventually conceded the Nov. 3 shooting of his new roommate, Kade Tuttle, 24, was "an impulsive thing" and acknowledged Tuttle "never made explicit threats of violence". Riedman, now charged with murder, had locked Tuttle out of their Salt Lake City apartment amid disputes over lights, food and items taken without permission, then fired once through the front door, according to the charges. Riedman initially told police he feared Tuttle would come in with others to hurt him, and he did not call for help after hearing a gurgling noise, the charges state.

item.title: Family mourns father killed in ATV accident, leaving 3 daughters without parents
item.description:
Hans Anderson's three daughters, who lost their mother eight years ago, are now without either parent after the 45-year-old died in an Oct. 31 side-by-side rollover on Strawberry Ridge above Hobble Creek Canyon. His sister, Janae Watson, said it was hard to accept that such a lifelong rider died this way, but she finds some comfort that it happened in the mountains he loved: "He died doing what he loved." The family has set up a GoFundMe for the daughters, the youngest of whom is 14.

item.title: Senators probing RFK Jr.'s testimony on Samoa trip after media documents refute it
item.description:
Democratic Sens. Ron Wyden and Angela Alsobrooks have opened an inquiry into whether Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health secretary, lied to Congress in saying his 2019 Samoa trip had "nothing to do with vaccines," after AP and Guardian reporting in August surfaced a letter he sent Samoa's prime minister that mentioned vaccine or vaccination eight times. Their letter to Children's Health Defense, the nonprofit known for anti-vaccine activism that Kennedy once chaired, seeks records on the trip, his 2024 campaign and his confirmation by Dec. 4. HHS has called claims based on the letters that Kennedy lied to Congress "outright defamatory", and while he was not under oath, knowingly giving false material testimony to Congress can still be a crime, though one rarely prosecuted.

item.title: US returns over $12 billion in oil proceeds to Venezuela since Maduro's ouster, report says
item.description:
A KPMG accounting released Thursday by the State Department says sales of Venezuelan crude, plus small amounts of gold, minerals and fertilizer, brought in $12.26 billion after Nicolás Maduro's ouster in January, and the Trump administration says nearly 99% has been returned to Venezuela. Under the energy deal with the interim authorities, proceeds go into a U.S.-managed account until Venezuelan officials win approval to use them for infrastructure and humanitarian needs; most moved through foreign exchange transactions with Venezuelan commercial banks, about $133 million went directly to services or supplies for the government, and approved payments included $5 million to law firm Greenberg Traurig. The report withholds the names of the 20 oil and gold buyers, though each was vetted for sanctions and money-laundering compliance, which the reporters call a sharp break from past practice.

item.title: US envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then head for Dublin to see Zelenskyy
item.description:
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner briefed Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin for about two hours after brokering two days of Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi that produced an agreement on a large prisoner swap but no major breakthrough, then flew to Dublin to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Kushner said the delegations "agreed on many of the principles," while Putin told the envoys that European troops in postwar Ukraine would be "absolutely unacceptable". Zelenskyy, who insisted Ukraine won't give up occupied territory for peace, also complained of new speed limits on the Starshield satellite service that he said a military investigation found were not random.

item.title: Google knows smart glasses have a privacy problem. Here's how it's trying to fix it
item.description:
Google's AI glasses built with Samsung, in frames from Warby Parker (from $395) and Gentle Monster (from $449), launch Dec. 10 with a tamper-resistant recording light, encrypted camera data and redaction of bystanders' faces in images sent to Gemini, though that blurring does not apply to ordinary photos and videos. Google's Juston Payne told CNN the company is researching more ways to warn bystanders as well as location-based limits, but said those measures remain in research and that a bare alert "can actually be weirdly disempowering" to the person being recorded. Privacy experts argue an LED is not enough protection, and Google's Shahram Izadi said the company has no plans to add facial recognition.

item.title: US Interior secretary visits Utah geothermal site, calls it example of 'energy dominance agenda'
item.description:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum toured Fervo's Cape geothermal station in Beaver County on Wednesday, calling it "a great example of President Trump's energy dominance agenda" and praising local support. The plant now generates about 33 megawatts for California customers, and Fervo plans to reach around 500 megawatts by 2028 and is in talks with Google about powering a possible hyperscale data center that could eventually push its output to some 8 gigawatts. Burgum said foreign influence has been behind efforts to turn communities against data centers, and he dismissed a ProPublica report that he stands to profit from the AI boom through his tech investments as "a complete false statement."

item.title: Families from France, US reunite in Veterans Day story 80 years in the making
item.description:
Richard Moseley of Kearns traveled to England and France to retrace the path of his father, 2nd Lt. Lonnie Moseley, a P-47 pilot who crashed under anti-aircraft fire in German-occupied France on July 4, 1944, and to meet the descendants of Lucien Lestang, the farmer who hid the wounded American in a barn for about six weeks. Lestang forged identity papers and passed the pilot off to German soldiers as a deaf mute farmhand, a risk Moseley said could have gotten the farmer's family and even the village executed. At the reunion, grandson Didier Lestang's home held a preserved piece of Lonnie's parachute, and Moseley said his father "called him his savior."

item.title: The historic SS United States is sunk after a long goodbye off Florida's coast
item.description:
The SS United States, the 1952 liner that was once the fastest ship afloat and is longer than the Titanic, was deliberately sunk Wednesday about 25 miles southwest of Destin, Florida, in a $13.5 million project to make it the world's largest artificial reef. The ship stayed visible for hours longer than organizers had predicted, which an Okaloosa County spokesperson attributed partly to crews flooding 128 fuel and lubricant tanks so it would settle evenly, before it tipped and went under around 9 p.m. "She is an amazing lady who will not lay down without a fight," said Coleen O'Malley, whose company handled the sinking, and the county, which aims to make the area the world's top spot for divers, expects the wreck to rest shallow enough for inexperienced divers to visit.

item.title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom as state's first Black US senator since Reconstruction
item.description:
Democrat Scott Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith after days of counting absentee and affidavit ballots, becoming Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction and the first new Democratic senator the state has chosen since 1947. The narrow result deepens what AP calls a decisive midterm rebuke of President Trump, with Colom drawing on strong Delta turnout, economic discontent and Hyde-Smith's missteps, including a beef-price remark he turned into an ad in which voters say they'd "pick another senator instead." Hyde-Smith, who had blocked Colom's 2022 nomination to the federal bench, conceded in a two-minute online video, saying "I respect the decision of Mississippi voters" and wishing Colom well.

item.title: For the first time, Utah Medicaid can help pay for Native American traditional healing
item.description:
Utah's Traditional Healing Demonstration has won federal approval, letting Medicaid help pay for certain traditional Native American healing services, which can range from sweat lodge ceremonies to talking circles, when provided through Indian Health Service, tribal or urban Indian health programs, making Utah one of six states with such approval. Matt Poss, executive director of the Urban Indian Center of Salt Lake, which revived its dormant sweat lodge about a year and a half ago with help from Ute healer Henry Howell, said the practices work alongside Western medicine, adding, "They all complement one another". Federal officials turned down Utah's request for a 100% federal match at urban Indian facilities, which will get the state's usual rate instead, and it has not been confirmed whether payments for the services have begun at the center.

item.title: Utah National Guard's Veterans Day concert brings together hundreds of student singers, veterans
item.description:
The Utah National Guard's 23rd Army Band and 480 Granite School District high school choir students performed for hundreds at the Tabernacle on Temple Square for the Guard's 71st annual Veterans Day Concert, which also honored students' award-winning essays about relatives who served. Gary Harter, a veteran who leads the Utah Department of Veterans and Military Affairs, tied the event to a long tradition of wartime music, from the Revolutionary War to Glenn Miller and Bing Crosby entertaining World War II troops. Seeing young people sing in tribute was especially meaningful, Harter said: "You like to think you did good while you were in the military as well."

item.title: CenturyLink is phasing out copper landlines in Utah
item.description:
As CenturyLink retires its copper landline network in Utah, a 50-year home customer and the owner of Salty Peaks Skate and Snowboard Shop say their lines went dead without adequate warning and their long-held phone numbers were lost, with owner Dennis Nazari calling it "a severe hit to the business". Parent company Lumen said both had been sent letters in advance and that numbers cannot be retrieved once service ends, though Nazari said the shop got its number back a day after KSL Investigators reached out to Lumen. CenturyLink shed much of its duty to keep copper lines running when lawmakers passed SB269 last year, after the Public Service Commission twice refused to release it as carrier of last resort, and Lumen plans to speed up the phaseout with notices starting next month.

item.title: Firefighters dig through rubble after NYC building collapse kills 2 and traps people in wreckage
item.description:
A three-story mixed-use building in Brooklyn's Flatbush section collapsed Wednesday afternoon into a neighboring lot being excavated for construction, leaving at least two dead and others buried under bricks and wood. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at least 10 people were hospitalized, four in critical condition, as about 250 firefighters dug by hand and with power saws and rescuers used dogs to find survivors, while FDNY chief of department John Esposito said "We do not know how many people were missing overall". FDNY officials said the search would go on for several days, and one resident told the New York Post that his wife and two young children, trapped in the rubble, were pulled out alive.

item.title: Man sentenced to prison for beating his roommate to death, seeks appeal
item.description:
Tyler James Vernon, convicted by a jury in November 2024 of murdering his 61-year-old roommate Steven Richard Nyce in a 2019 beating, was sentenced Oct. 15 to 15 years to life, with credit recommended for more than seven and a half years already served. The roughly two-year wait for sentencing stemmed partly from Vernon's unsuccessful bid to arrest the verdict, and Third District Judge Todd Shaughnessy later rejected a new-trial request too, writing that there was "ample admissible evidence" of the required mental state despite Vernon's drug use. Vernon appealed that ruling, and on Tuesday the Utah Supreme Court moved it to the Utah Court of Appeals.

item.title: Bipartisan coalition pushes for new oversight of license plate reader systems in Utah
item.description:
A bipartisan coalition that includes the Lehi-based Libertas Institute is working on legislation that would require warrants before police search automatic license plate reader databases in active criminal investigations, with exceptions for stolen-vehicle hot lists, missing persons and emergencies such as kidnappings. The coalition also wants independent third-party audits, which Libertas privacy analyst Emily Grimmius said the KSL Investigators' report this week shows are needed: a former Tooele County detective used the system to look up the car of a man whose estranged wife the detective was dating, misuse that no routine internal audit caught. "Internal checks are great, but as we've clearly identified through the story you broke, they're not enough," Grimmius said, noting more than 300 documented misuse cases nationally but none in Utah until KSL's story.

item.title: BYU students search for lost veterans decades later
item.description:
Scot Chipman's father, Marine A-6 pilot Jim Chipman, was killed over North Vietnam in December 1972, and his remains came home to American Fork in 2023 through the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency effort that BYU students now support with records research and relatives' DNA. BYU's Suzanne Adams, who directs its Center for Family History and Genealogy, urged families still searching to register as next of kin at dpaa.mil, and BYU reported its work most recently helped return two airmen, Lt. item.title: After surviving war, Utah veteran's new mission is helping others find a way forward
item.description:
After surviving eight roadside bomb blasts in Iraq and later losing a close friend and fellow soldier to suicide, retired Army Sgt. Josh Hansen and his wife, Melissa, founded Continue Mission in 2014, a Utah nonprofit offering free hiking, skiing, pickleball and other outings that let registered veterans connect with peers. VA data cited in the story put Utah's 2024 veteran suicide deaths at 65 and show that 62% of veterans who died by suicide that year had gone without VA health care in that year or the prior one, though the VA found Utah's higher unadjusted rate was not statistically significant once age was considered. Hansen, who stresses that recreation is no substitute for professional care, said "The reason our organization works is the networking," as introductions grow into friendships outside the group.

Ogden police unveiled an administrative order Tuesday, in effect since Oct. 19, that bars officers from asking people about their immigration status and spells out when they may assist federal immigration agents, after two late-summer ICE detentions involving Ogden officers were caught on video and drew backlash. Chief Jake Sube told the City Council that immigrants "do not have to fear calling us" and pleaded with crime victims to contact police, while Capt. Mayor Ben Nadolski said there is "legitimate reason to be concerned" about how federal immigration policies are being carried out, and Councilwoman Alicia Washington thanked police for the policy while voicing concern about the Weber County Sheriff's Office's 287(g) agreement with ICE.

item.title: BYU-led study points to potential reason for mule deer population decline in the West
item.description:
A study led by Brigham Young University with the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources and conservation groups found that managing mule deer herds for a higher share of males is associated with poorer nutrition in females and slower population growth. Drawing on 15 years of productivity data and seven years of body-reserve measurements, researchers saw less fat on does in high male-ratio areas, which co-author Brock McMillan said may stem from food competition with larger bucks and from females being chased during the rut. McMillan called the result a "game changer" that "could partially explain the population decline of mule deer over the last 30 or 40 years throughout the West", while acknowledging the public and wildlife managers may be slow to accept it.

Third District Judge Theresa Welch sent Deon Jennings to prison for one to 15 years for the 2022 stabbing death of Willie Houston, 59, his aunt's boyfriend, turning down defense requests to lower the offense to a third-degree felony and impose five years of probation instead. Intermountain Health is rolling out a program called Safe Infant Sleep, with free consultations at Primary Children's campuses in Lehi and Salt Lake, where trained ambassadors tailor safe-sleep advice to each family's home and caregiver wellbeing is a central focus. A state health department report counted 137 sudden unexpected infant deaths in Utah from 2019 to 2023, roughly 27 a year. Of those deaths, Intermountain neonatal ICU medical director Jessica Davidson said, "About 93% of them were in an unsafe sleep environment", with many infants found on soft bedding, on surfaces not designed for sleep or on their stomachs.

item.description:

Hopes rest partly on a super El Niño and on Utah's wettest July-through-October stretch since at least 1895, and KSL meteorologist Matt Johnson expects the active storm pattern to continue, though long-range forecasts reveal little yet about temperatures, a big factor in last year's shortfall. item.description:
Unions said 4 million Spanish workers joined Wednesday's general strike over the country's housing affordability crisis, the first since a 2012 walkout against austerity, with pickets braving storms less than three weeks before a Nov. 29 snap election. Spain is short about 750,000 homes, according to the central bank, and the Youth Council of Spain says average rent equals roughly 98.7% of a young person's monthly salary; "I'm 36 years old and I still can't move out on my own," said Jesus Gonzalez, who works in a Madrid hospital IT department. item.title: Salt Lake man pleads guilty to possessing more than 200 explicits photos of children
item.description:
Brennan Christopher Bennett, a 42-year-old Salt Lake man, pleaded guilty Monday in federal court to receipt of child sex abuse material, admitting he had 235 images and seven videos on a Samsung flip phone. The case began when FBI agents searched his apartment in October 2025 and found four firearms he was barred from owning because of a 2021 conviction for attempted enticement of a minor, in which he had arranged to meet an undercover officer posing as a 13-year-old. Under the plea agreement Bennett is likely to get almost 11 years in prison plus lifetime probation, with sentencing set for Jan. 25.

item.title: Utah County woman shares domestic abuse survival story
item.description:
Emilee Jordan, who met Isaac Steffens Rowley on Snapchat after graduating from high school in 2025, told KSL he seemed charming around others but was "just a monster" in private, repeatedly assaulting and choking her until a secret text to her mother brought police to his home in March. American Fork Detective Ashleigh Gutierrez said Rowley first tried to deflect by reporting Jordan for extortion, and recorded jail calls show him planning to convince her he still loved her, which Gutierrez described as an effort to keep manipulating her from behind bars. Rowley, 23, pleaded guilty in August to charges including aggravated kidnapping and aggravated assault and will serve at least 10 years, and Jordan says she spoke out so others will leave abusive relationships.

item.title: Greta Thunberg warns 'everything we love is at stake' as she arrives at UN climate talks
item.description:
Greta Thunberg arrived Tuesday at the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, her first U.N. summit since Glasgow in 2021, saying host countries use the talks each year to "whitewash themselves" and warning that "everything and everyone we love is at stake." The summit follows a year of deadly heat waves and floods plus an energy shock from the Iran war, and co-hosts Turkey and Australia are promoting renewables while still leaning heavily on coal; Turkey wants electricity to supply 35% of global energy use by 2035, up from 23%. Her arrival excited many youth climate activists, and Amber Turner of the Alliance of Small Island States voiced hope that Thunberg's presence would remind people why they took up the cause; the talks run until Nov. 20.

item.title: Utah's household debt is up 34%. Is that bad news for our wallets?
item.description:
Some 9.45% of Utah credit card balances are 90 or more days past due, compared with 5.84% in 2019, and overall household debt in the state has grown 34% over the same span, a pace exceeded only by Idaho and well above the roughly 23% national rise, according to Smart Debt Relief analyses. Utah Valley University financial planning professor Shane Stewart says housing costs are what most people are feeling, and while a mortgage can build wealth, buyers should ask whether a home will leave them "home poor". Stewart ties the borrowing partly to confidence in a strong state economy, noting, "Consumer sentiment is powerful".

item.title: Tech consultant sentenced to 16 years to life in stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee
item.description:
A San Francisco judge sentenced tech consultant Nima Momeni to 16 years to life Tuesday for the 2023 stabbing death of Cash App creator Bob Lee, after denying his request for a new trial; his attorneys plan to appeal. A jury convicted Momeni of second-degree murder in December 2024, rejecting both his self-defense claim and the first-degree charge, after prosecutors argued he was angry that Lee had connected his sister with a drug dealer who, she says, drugged and sexually assaulted her. Lee's 18-year-old daughter, Scout, told Momeni in court that he had "ended an entire future built around a man," according to media reports, while Momeni said the two sides had completely different understandings of what happened.

item.title: After bond fails, Sandy mayor defends process of putting issue to residents
item.description:
Sandy Mayor Monica Zoltanski said she would still put the purchase of Crescent View Middle School to voters even after the $30 million bond failed 51-48 on Election Night, arguing residents deserved to decide rather than learn of the deal afterward. Zoltanski, who backed the bond, blamed a short education window, economic "headwinds" such as gas prices and tariffs, and the gap between the $17 million price for the school and its 17 acres and the larger bond amount set by the city council, which she called "too high." Canyons School District will now return to interested developers, and Zoltanski plans to ask lawmakers for a preferred rate so cities need not match private bids for district land.

item.title: Whose DNA is it? Legal analyst says unanswered question could loom over Douglas Carter trial
item.description:
Prosecutors say they will keep pursuing the 1985 murder case against Douglas Carter, 71, a former death row inmate whose conviction was overturned in 2025 over police and prosecutorial misconduct, and whom later DNA testing excluded as the source of evidence including DNA from the murder weapon. At a Provo hearing Tuesday, Carter's attorneys pressed for more testing to identify whose DNA it is, and KSL legal analyst Greg Skordas said a jury would likely ask the same thing, calling the results "a pretty big blow to the state's case, but it's not a fatal blow" if prosecutors have enough other evidence, such as his confession. Judge Derek Pullan is expected to rule by Dec. 11 on the defense's bid to suppress that confession as coerced, and Carter remains free under pretrial supervision.

item.title: Saratoga Springs schools temporarily locked down after police chase alleged carjacker
item.description:
Police arrested a man in Saratoga Springs on Tuesday after a pursuit during which police placed five schools there on secure status from 8:32 to 8:49 a.m., the Alpine School District said. Sandy police Sgt. Michael Olsen said the suspect, in his 20s, had fired a shot at the ground during a failed carjacking attempt that morning in Salt Lake City and later took another woman's Nissan, which the carmaker helped officers track through Herriman to Lehi, where he ran. Nobody was hurt, Olsen said, and the man had not been identified.

item.title: Indigenous Student Union hosts Heritage Week at SUU
item.description:
A turquoise day Wednesday, a traditional attire day Friday and the Miss Indigenous Princess Pageant on Saturday round out Southern Utah University's annual Heritage Week, which the Indigenous Student Union launched Monday with childhood coyote stories to open Native American Heritage Month. The union, which also hosted a Navajo taco lunch, is performing Thursday for private donors at the Southern Utah Museum of Art. Union president Kaeahliyah Howard, a Navajo (Diné) senior, said the week helps Indigenous students feel represented and connected, but the events are open to all because "Indigenous Student Union is for everyone".

item.title: Driver accused of hitting woman changing flat showed no remorse, prosecutors say
item.description:
Prosecutors on Tuesday charged Peter Joseph Hoffelmeyer, 47, of Herriman, with automobile homicide in the Oct. 30 death of Taylor Breanne Giles, 36, of Sandy, who was struck while changing a flat on the westbound I-80 shoulder in Parley's Canyon. Troopers found no sign of hard braking and Giles' phone displaying tire-changing instructions, and charges say Hoffelmeyer, driving back from a Park City Halloween party, blew 0.144% on a breath test and told a trooper he "definitely had alcohol in his system". Prosecutors wrote that he never showed "concern or remorse" for Giles during the investigation.

item.title: Eisenkot unveils agenda to reverse Netanyahu's policies as Israel's new parliament is sworn in
item.description:
As Israel's new Knesset was sworn in Tuesday, Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief tasked with forming a government, vowed to undo many of Benjamin Netanyahu's policies, and his bloc filed bills for an official Oct. 7 inquiry, prime ministerial term limits and a reversal of the outgoing government's judicial changes. Netanyahu, who has made unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties stole the election, used a post-ceremony speech to cast Arab lawmakers as untrustworthy, prompting Eisenkot to call it "divisive" and "hate-filled" and cancel a planned meeting with Likud. Eisenkot has up to six weeks to build a coalition, while opponents who now hold a solid majority began moving to oust Netanyahu-backed speaker Amir Ohana in favor of Yashar's Matan Kahana, a vote that could come as early as this week.
